Seven men: a number sufficient for this ministry, and one of the sacred numbers that signify the work of the Holy Spirit, such as the seven sacraments of the Church.
Of honest report: known for uprightness and justice.
Full of the Holy Ghost: this appears in their devout life and their righteousness.
Wisdom: good conduct.
We may appoint: by prayer and the laying on of the Apostles' hands upon them.
This business: the distribution of gifts to the needy among the members of the Church.
The Apostles asked the people to choose seven to be set apart for this ministry, in whom certain conditions are met, namely being full of the Holy Spirit and of service.
Then the Church, that is, the Apostles, played their part in ordaining them and consecrating them to the ministry of distribution. Thus the procedure was in spirituality, democracy and wisdom.
The Apostles devote themselves to leading the corporate prayers and to preaching.
The saying pleased: the members of the Church were pleased with the counsel of the Apostles to choose seven to arrange and organize the material distribution in the Church.

All agreed on this and chose the seven, the first of whom was Stephen. Stephen: he was distinguished in his righteousness, and became the first martyr of Christianity (ch. 7:60). Philip: he is the one who preached in Samaria and baptized the Ethiopian eunuch (ch. 8:26-39), and afterward preached in Caesarea, and he had four virgin daughters who prophesied (ch. 21:8). Nicolas: who was not of Jewish origin, but a proselyte from Antioch, and who afterward became the founder of the heresy mentioned in the Book of Revelation (Rev 2:15).
The prayers of ordination were carried out with the laying on of hands, which the Church took as an ancient tradition for the transmission of priestly authority.

Here is a clear proclamation of the sacrament of the priesthood in the ordination of one of the ranks of the priesthood, which is the diaconate, and it has continued in the Church ever since in the ordination of the three degrees of the priesthood, the episcopate, the presbyterate and the diaconate, by the laying on of the bishops' hands on those who come forward for this service.
The word of God increased: the spread of the preaching of Christ.

The Church passed through the problem, and the number of believers in Jerusalem increased until it included for the first time a company of the Jewish priests, who were perhaps deeply affected by the tearing of the veil of the Temple on the day of the Crucifixion of Christ and felt the end of worship in the Temple, and who lost their position and their source of livelihood for their faith in Christ, whom they felt to be better than everything.

Because of Stephen's strong faith, in addition to his ministry in distributing gifts he helped the Apostles in preaching and teaching, and God strengthened him by working miracles, which drew many to faith.

Do not be disturbed if problems face you, and trust that the Holy Spirit is able to solve them. Take refuge in God in prayer, and rely on the guidance of your father of confession and the spiritual fathers, and think in a positive way, and God will solve all your problems.

Satan and the leaders of the Jews stirred up the members of some synagogues in Jerusalem, in which at this time there were many synagogues for preaching. Each group of the Jews living in foreign countries had synagogues in which they attended when they visited Jerusalem at the feasts and on pilgrimages, and this synagogue was one of them. The Libertines: Jews who had been captured in Rome as slaves and were then given their freedom by the Romans. The Cyrenians: from North Africa (Libya). The Alexandrians: that is, the Jews of Alexandria, whose number at that time reached about a million. Those of Cilicia: in Turkey, lying between Tarsus, the city of Saul (later Paul), and Asia, that is, western Turkey.

These began to dispute with Stephen, but they were not able to resist the wisdom of the Holy Spirit speaking on his tongue, and the evidence and proofs he presented from the books of the Old Testament.
They suborned men: they agreed with some Jews on false testimony against Stephen, and went in among those present in the synagogue and stirred them up and incited them against him.
Moses: against the Law of Moses, because he taught that these were types of the law of the New Testament.
God: because he taught that Christ is God, so they considered that blasphemy.

These Jews, as their leaders had earlier at the trial of Christ, resorted to intrigue and falsification through some of their men who had attended Stephen's sermons, and claimed that he was blaspheming Moses and God.
They stirred up the people: the group of Jews in revolt against Stephen disturbed and agitated the people, whether those gathered in the synagogue or those they visited in their homes.
The elders: the members of the Sanhedrin.

The scribes: those responsible for copying the books of the Old Testament, who were among the leaders of the people. The council: the Sanhedrin or council of the seventy elders, responsible for issuing decisions and judging the accused in religious matters.
They continued in their plan to stir up the people against him, as did the leaders of the Jews and the scribes, who in turn seized Stephen to be tried for that before the Sanhedrin.
Ceaseth not: continuing in teachings against the Jewish law.
This holy place: the Sanhedrin was meeting in one of the porches of the Temple, and what is meant by the place is the Jewish Temple.
Here false witnesses came forward testifying to Stephen's repeated offense against the dignity of the Temple and the Mosaic Law.

The witnesses said they had heard him themselves say that the Lord Christ, whom they called the Nazarene in order to disparage Him, because nothing good comes out of Nazareth (Jn 1:46), as they said in their proverbs, would destroy the Temple and change its rites, as they had said at the trial of Christ.
At the beginning of the trial, Stephen was calm in his features, his face shining, without fear or pride or fanaticism, like an angel.

Truly God appears in the conduct of His children and on their features, and this is a measure of God's dwelling in our hearts, for a joyful heart makes a cheerful countenance (Prov 15:13). So repeat inwardly prayers and psalms that give you an inner calm that shows on your features, and you will be a silent proclamation to everyone who sees you. Stephen's defense and stoning

entries.section: (1) From Abraham to his father Moses

paragraphs.text: The trial of Stephen was about seven years after the Ascension of Christ, and the high priest asked Stephen to defend himself against the charge of blasphemy against Moses, God and the Temple, with which they had accused him.

entries.section: (1) From Abraham to his father Moses

paragraphs.text: Haran: a city lying west of the Euphrates in Iraq, north of Ur of the Chaldees.
The land that I shall show you: he means the land of Canaan, which is the region of the Jordan and Palestine, and He did not name it in order to test Abraham's reliance and obedience.

Stephen began with a preaching address, and the remarkable thing is that he did not defend himself at all, but set about a preaching effort toward the Jews, recounting their history to them to win them to his side, so that he could persuade them to believe in Christ. Despite their ill intentions toward him, Stephen addressed them with the utmost respect and called them brethren and fathers. During his address Stephen was showing them that God has many holy places in the world besides the Jewish Temple, whose destruction they considered blasphemy; so he told them that God appeared to Abraham between the Tigris and the Euphrates in his town, Ur of the Chaldees, to call him, and did not appear to him in Jerusalem.

entries.section: (1) From Abraham to his father Moses

paragraphs.text: The land of the Chaldeans: the city of Ur of the Chaldees.
This land, wherein you now dwell: Canaan.

Our father Abraham responded to the call of God, but his father Terah held on to him and went out with him, so he obeyed him and settled in Haran until Terah died, and God appeared to Abraham a second time and called him to the land of Canaan, and he obeyed.

entries.section: (1) From Abraham to his father Moses

paragraphs.text: God promised that the land would belong to the seed of Abraham, who in his lifetime did not possess any of it, and Abraham had no children at the time of the promise.

entries.section: (1) From Abraham to his father Moses

paragraphs.text: He informed him that his seed would be strangers in Egypt for about four hundred years, in many insults and troubles; and that was fulfilled.

entries.section: (1) From Abraham to his father Moses

paragraphs.text: God judges Pharaoh and the Egyptians for their wickedness. Then the sons of Abraham come out and worship God in the land of Canaan and not in Jerusalem, which they regarded as the summit of holiness.

entries.section: (1) From Abraham to his father Moses

paragraphs.text: Circumcision was the sign of the covenant between God and Abraham and his seed, and Abraham performed circumcision on Isaac on the eighth day from his birth as God commanded, an indication of the connection of the promise with eternal life, symbolized by the number "8" in the Holy Bible, because it comes after "7," the symbol of the time of the creation of the world.

Then came Jacob and the heads of the tribes, who envied Joseph their brother and sold him to Egypt, and that is a symbol of their envy of Christ and their selling Him to the Romans to kill Him, but God was with him.

entries.section: (1) From Abraham to his father Moses

paragraphs.text: God rescued Joseph from Potiphar's wife and from prison, and blessed him until he stood before the king of Egypt, who made him his first minister, responsible for the care and administration of all Egypt. By this Joseph is a type of Christ, who chose suffering and died for us and then rose to be the shepherd and head of the Church and of all His people.

entries.section: (1) From Abraham to his father Moses

paragraphs.text: Food: for them and for their cattle.
Our fathers: ten of his sons, namely those other than Joseph and Benjamin.

The first time: as in (Gen 45:4). When the famine began in Egypt and extended to Canaan and the whole world, hunger and distress reached the heads of the tribes also, so their father Jacob sent them to Egypt to get wheat.

entries.section: (1) From Abraham to his father Moses

paragraphs.text: Then he sent them a second time (Gen 45:16), when Joseph made himself known to them and Pharaoh learned of the whole family of Joseph.

entries.section: (1) From Abraham to his father Moses

paragraphs.text: Joseph sent and summoned his father and all his brothers and their families to Egypt, and their total number was about 75 souls.

entries.section: (1) From Abraham to his father Moses

paragraphs.text: Jacob and his sons lived in Egypt until they died there, and likewise Joseph.

entries.section: (1) From Abraham to his father Moses

paragraphs.text: When the people went out of Egypt they took the bones of their fathers, the heads of the tribes, and buried some of them in the cave of the field that Abraham bought from the sons of Heth, in which he was buried with Sarah and his son Isaac, and others in the tomb that Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor in Shechem in Samaria, and with them were the bones of Joseph also.

Stephen combined the two places bought by Abraham and Jacob, which are the two fields bought from the sons of Heth and from the sons of Hamor at Shechem in Samaria, so he said the field that Abraham bought in Shechem, meaning the two fields.

entries.section: (1) From Abraham to his father Moses

paragraphs.text: The time of the promise: the time of the fulfillment of God's promise to bring His people out of Egypt.
Which knew not Joseph: he did not appreciate the kindness and services of Joseph to Egypt.
Dealt subtilly: by trying to kill the males of the children of Israel by means of the two midwives, and then by casting them into the Nile, so that the people of God would grow weak.
Cast out: rejected from life by being killed after their birth.

The people of Israel were increasing greatly in number in Egypt, so that one of the kings who ruled after Joseph (most likely Rameses II, who was not a contemporary of Joseph but of course had heard of his story) tried by various means and wicked devices to do away with the Jews of Egypt by killing their male children as soon as they were born, so that they would die out.

Truly Satan fights the Church and tries to end its seed, but God always rescues His people at the right time. So do not be troubled by the agitation of the wicked, however strong they may seem, because God Himself protects you, and His blessing to you even increases in the days of distress and persecution.
At which time: the time of the royal command to cast the Jewish male children into the river Nile as soon as they were born.
His father's: Amram.
Moses the prophet was born in 1571 BC, and his parents kept him three months in their house, thereby disobeying the king's command, out of their love for him and his beauty.

His parents were afterward forced to cast him into the Nile, but God arranged that one of the daughters of Pharaoh of Egypt, who had no children, should draw him out, and she adopted him as her son and raised him in the royal palace.

Moses grew up in the royal palace, learning the highest sciences of Egypt, which was famous at that time for learning and philosophy, so he became advanced in knowledge and distinguished in his conduct and works.

When Moses reached the age of forty, God put it in his mind to take care of his brethren the Jews, to visit them and ask after them, because the Egyptians, among whom Moses was counted as one, did not mingle with the Jews.

Moses saw an Egyptian wronging a Jew, so he tried to defend the Jew and remove the wrong from him, and killed the Egyptian, and he thought that the Jews would appreciate his mission to rescue them from the wrong of the Egyptians, but they rejected him when he tried to settle the quarrel between two of them, and the wrongdoer pushed him away, saying, who has set you up with authority over us?

This is a type of what the Jews did to the Lord Christ, for they did not understand that He was the Savior, but objected to Him, saying through their rulers, "By what authority doest thou these things?" (Mt 21:23).

The Jews reproached Moses and accused him of being a murderer, and thereby they could hand him over to Pharaoh to take vengeance on him and kill him. Likewise the Jews reproached Christ and insulted Him.
Moses fled from all of Egypt, and went to where the sons of Abraham by Keturah (the Midianites) were living, east of the Gulf of Aqaba, and there he married and had two sons, Gershom and Eliezer.
Moses lived there another forty years, until God appeared to him in the form of an angel in the flame of the bush in the wilderness, which was burning and was not consumed.
A voice: God did not appear in any form, but His voice was speaking from the burning bush.
Moses marveled at the sight and drew near to examine it, and God addressed him, saying:

I am the God of your fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, so that Moses would understand that God is a lover of mankind to the degree that He calls Himself their God and rejoices in that, and because He would fulfill His promises to them by freeing them from the bondage of Egypt. So Moses was afraid and hid his eyes from the majesty of God.

God asked him to take off his shoes (as the priests later came to do during their ministry in the Jewish Temple, and as we do now in the church because its ground is holy ground). Thus Stephen indicated that there are holy grounds outside the Temple and Jerusalem, against which they accused him of blasphemy. The Temple is holy, and God also sanctified other places such as the one where He appeared to Moses in the bush, and Christ sanctifies in the New Testament many places such as the churches.
The affliction of my people: the pains of slavery and forced labor in Egypt.
Their groaning: their suffering and crying out to God to save them.
I am come down to deliver them: an expression according to human understanding to show that He will save them.
God declared that He would come to Egypt to rescue His people from Pharaoh, because He had heard their prayer and answered it, and He asked Moses to go to Egypt.
God's coming down to Egypt is a symbol of His Incarnation, in order to bind Satan by His cross and redeem us.

By the hand of the angel: God presents Himself in the form of an angel so that men can bear to speak with Him, but it is clear from the voice that came from the bush that it was the speech of God Himself.

Stephen returns to assure them that they, that is, their forefathers, resisted Moses in his saving ministry although God had sent him as a ruler, just as He later sent His Son as Ruler and Savior, yet they rejected Him. Likewise the Coptic Church still joins the Incarnation with the story of the bush in the hymns and praises of the month of Kiahk.
In the land of Egypt: that is, the ten plagues.
In the Red Sea: when he divided it with the rod, and it is also called Yam Suph. It was called the Red Sea because of the red weeds in it and the red sands and mountains beside it.
In the wilderness: such as the coming down of the manna and the quails.

Moses accomplished the mission in spite of that, as the Son accomplished salvation, and brought them out of the bondage of Pharaoh, working the ten wonderful plagues and many miracles and signs, that is, the marks that confirm he was sent from God (Ex 4:1-9), and he divided the Red Sea and led them on the wilderness journey to the border of the Promised Land for another forty years.

Stephen pointed to the prophecy of Moses in the Book of Deuteronomy (Deut 18:15-18) about Christ the Savior who would come sent from God from among the Jewish people, and Moses charged them to listen to Him, but they did not listen to Him, and resisted Him as they did Moses himself.
The church in the wilderness: he means the assembly of God with His people in the wilderness under the leadership of Moses and Aaron.

This is the Moses who led them by the power of the angel of the bush (God the Word) on the wilderness journey, and to whom He spoke on Mount Sinai and all along the journey, giving him life-giving words and commandments to deliver to them.
The Jews refused to obey him, but wanted to put him aside and return to Egypt, to which they were attached although they had come out of it.

The children of Israel asked Aaron to make them idols to worship, and refused to let the Lord go before them in the pillar of fire or cloud, preferring the idols to God, claiming that Moses had been lost on the mountain while he was receiving the two tablets of the covenant.
They made a calf: Aaron made from the gold that the Jews gave him an image of a calf, as the Egyptians used to worship the calf Apis.
The works of their own hands: because many shared in making the calf and organizing festivals and worship for it.
Gave them up: He abandoned them, so they went astray and worshiped created things, perhaps that they might return when they grew tired of their error.

The book of the prophets: the Jews gathered the books of the prophets into one book which they called the Book of the Prophets. Have ye offered: a rhetorical question meaning that they did not offer worship to God only but to idols also. The Lord was angry and delivered them to their enemies because they worshiped the stars and idols, as the prophet Amos prophesied in his prophecy (Amos 5:25-26), declaring their worship of idols throughout the wilderness journey.

Although the Tent of Meeting existed for the worship of God, they also carried with them small shrines containing an image of an idol named Moloch, easy to carry on the journey for worshiping the idol, and they worshiped another idol in the form of a star named Saturn (Remphan). This Moloch is the god of the sons of Ammon (the descendants of Lot), for whom Solomon the son of David built a shrine (1 Kgs 11:7) when he went astray from the worship of God because of his idolatrous wives, and he had a bronze image which they heated by lighting a fire under its outstretched arms, and then they offered their children to it as an offering by placing them on these two arms to be burned as a sacrifice to the idol, so God was angry and decreed their captivity to Babylon.
God does great miracles for us, yet we still resist Him as those did?! May we contemplate God's gifts and blessings in our lives, that we may thank Him every day and obey His commandments.

The Tent of Meeting contained the ark with the two tablets of the testimony inside it (on which the Ten Commandments were written), so it came to be called the tabernacle of witness, and Moses made it according to the pattern that the Lord showed him on the mountain.
Brought in: into the Promised Land.

Succeeded to: the sons held to it after the fathers, and inherited the worship of God through it. The possession of the Gentiles: in the Promised Land, where the children of Israel took possession in place of the peoples who had lived in these places.

The Jews took this tent by inheritance from the generation of Moses to the generation of Joshua and afterward, when they entered the Promised Land, which belonged to the Gentiles whom God drove out before the Jews, until the days of David.
Desired to find a tabernacle: he wanted to build a permanent house for God in place of the portable tent, and prepared the building materials.

Solomon built Him: God refused to let David build the house, because he had been in many wars and killed many, so He allowed his son, who lived in a time of peace, to build the Temple, in which they took great pride.
Dwelleth not: His presence is not confined to the Temple.
The prophet: Isaiah (Isa 66:1-2). God declared that He does not dwell in a building but first in the hearts of His children who believe in Him (Rom 8:11).
Heaven and earth cannot contain Him, so He does not rest in any house, however magnificent, but in the hearts of His children, because He is the maker of all houses and all their costly materials.

Here Stephen changed his style from the preceding historical presentation to rebuking his hearers, perhaps because he felt their distress at his words, which showed on their faces, so he was compelled to confront them quickly so that they would repent before they interrupted him and refused to hear the rest of his words; so he declared to them the hardness of their hearts, which had accompanied them throughout their history, so that their worship and their circumcision were outward and apparent only, and did not touch their hearts or their ears so that they would listen to Christ, and they lived resisting the voice of the Holy Spirit like their fathers.

The Jews rejected the witness of the Holy Spirit about Christ in the prophecies of the prophets of the Old Testament, and even killed the prophets and persecuted them, as Christ said in the parable of the vineyard (Lk 20:9-17), and they were the wicked husbandmen, trying to obliterate the prophecies the prophets had spoken about the incarnation of the Just One (Christ). And when He came they handed Him over to the Romans to kill Him, according to the counsel, opinion and suggestion of the Jews.
The Jews did not keep what they had received of the laws and commandments from Moses, to whom God delivered these commandments on the holy mountain by the hands of angels.

So man loses every blessing when he refuses to obey the Holy Bible delivered to him by God and continues in his error according to the evil of his thoughts. So accept the word of God that you read every day as a personal message to you, and apply it in your life.

(43) The martyrdom of Stephen (vv. 54-60), ch. 8:1 54 When they heard these things, they were enraged in their hearts, and they gnashed on him with their teeth. 55 But he, being full of the Holy Ghost, looked up steadfastly into heaven, and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God, 56 And said, "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing on the right hand of God." 57 Then they cried out with a loud voice, and stopped their ears, and ran upon him with one accord, 58 And cast him out of the city, and stoned him: and the witnesses laid down their clothes at a young man's feet, whose name was Saul. 59 And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." 60 And he kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." And when he had said this, he fell asleep. Ch. 8:1 And Saul was consenting unto his death. And at that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria, except the apostles.

Here their anger at Stephen reached its extreme because he had exposed the state of their wicked hearts, and their anger showed on their faces, so they gnashed their teeth because of their intense rage at him.
The right hand of God: that is, in the fullness of divine glory and majesty, for God has no right hand since He is unlimited.

After Stephen finished his sermon, and saw the wickedness of the Jews and their intentions to take vengeance on him, he felt that his mission had been completed, so he lifted his eyes toward heaven, beseeching God to support him, being filled with the Holy Spirit, and God showed him a comforting vision, for he saw heaven opened and the glory of God appearing in it, and the Lord Jesus standing in glory at the right hand of God to comfort and encourage him; and he declared to the hearers this great vision, which was the vision of Christ in His glory in heaven.

Here they did not wait for the council's verdict, but stopped their ears lest they hear from him what they counted as blasphemy, and with loud shouting they rushed upon him, proclaiming his blasphemy and his deserving death, and many accusations they were shouting.
They laid down their clothes: so that their hands might move freely for the stoning, and Saul of Tarsus kept their clothes until they had finished their task.
A young man: his age was between thirty and forty, because he was a member of the council, whose members could not be younger than thirty.

Saul: this is Saul of Tarsus who persecuted the Christians and later became the Apostle Paul. He was a member of the aforementioned synagogue that rose up against Stephen, because Tarsus is in the region of Cilicia.

They cast him out of Jerusalem lest he defile it, and stoned him with stones without a lawful verdict. The witnesses began the stoning according to the Law, that they might bear the consequence of their testimony if it was unjust.

While the Jews were stoning Stephen, he was calm, praying, asking God to receive his spirit to dwell with Him in heaven, and this shows the strength of his faith and his steadfastness in the last moments of his life.
Fell asleep: death is called sleep because it is a rest, for the spirit's transfer to God and its happiness with Him, and a rest for man from the toils of life.

Stephen knelt on his knees and prayed, asking forgiveness for those who stoned him, as his Lord Jesus Christ did on the Cross (Lk 23:34). Thus he ended his life with prayer, and his spirit was lifted up into the arms of Jesus Christ.
These feelings are the mark of Christians, for they love their enemies and ask God's forgiveness for them even while enduring the utmost torture from them.

Take care to complete your mission in life by witnessing for Christ and drawing those around you to Him, and whatever distress you endure, trust that Christ is beside you encouraging you and has prepared for you a great place in heaven. Ch. 8:1: St. Luke here declares that Saul of Tarsus was still persecuting the Christians up to this time, for he was among those who rose up against Stephen and condemned him to death. Persecution, dispersion and examples of preaching. This chapter is the beginning of the third part of the Book of Acts, which speaks of the persecution of the Church in Jerusalem, the dispersion that occurred and the appearance of the churches of the Gentiles.

After the killing of Stephen there began a severe persecution of the Christians of Jerusalem, with imprisonment, plunder and flogging of the believers, but God turned it to good, for the believers were scattered throughout all the villages of Judea and Samaria, that is, the southern and middle parts of the country. They chose Samaria because its people were naturally at enmity with the Jews, so they could not hand over the fleeing Christians to the Jews of Jerusalem. As for the Apostles, they would not leave Jerusalem, and stood firm to prove the steadfastness of the faith of the newborn Church.

Some devout Jewish men came and carried the body of Stephen, and made great lamentation over him to declare their displeasure at his killing, for they felt that he was righteous and did not deserve death, although they did not yet believe in the Christian faith.
The Christians were keeping away and hiding because of the Jewish persecution rising against them.

As for Saul: he was a Jew, whose name in Latin means "the important one," of the tribe of Benjamin, from the city of Tarsus, born at the beginning of the first Christian century, so that his age was then about forty years. He had studied in the famous school of Tarsus, like the school of Alexandria and the school of Athens. Saul was consenting to the persecution of the Christians that was going on, and took part in it by raiding the Church to steal what was in it and what the believers had of money, and he seized them and imprisoned them.
The word: Christ Jesus.
As for the Christians who were scattered from Jerusalem, in their wanderings they were not afraid of the Jews but were preaching the word despite the persecution that had befallen them.

Philip the deacon, one of the companions of the martyr Stephen, came down from Jerusalem, which is raised high on the mountains, to the land of Samaria, which is the middle part of the land of the Jews, and began to preach Christ to them.

There was an intense and collective response to his preaching, for they remembered Christ's preaching among them and His meeting with the Samaritan woman about 7 years before. They were impressed by the words of the preaching and amazed at the signs that accompanied it, such as the evil spirits coming out of those possessed by them, the spirits crying out with a great, terrifying voice at the power of the name of Christ. Many who were palsied (paralyzed) and lame were also healed.
Joy came to the city through the new faith and the great healing miracles.

Truly the Lord turns sorrow into joy and spiritual gain, and controls all the events of life to work for our salvation as long as we love Him (Rom 8:28). So do not be disturbed by afflictions, for God turns them to your good.

Simon the sorcerer lived in the town of Samaria, and he was the head of a heresy that spread afterward, called "al-Tursisiyyah," in which he claimed that he was the Son of God and that he was the Holy Spirit, and the Samaritans were amazed at his satanic miracles.
All followed him as a great man, thinking that he did this because he represented the power of God, and since he had had a long time, he succeeded in drawing many.
The things concerning the Kingdom of God: the reign of God over hearts, and His work in the believers within His Church through the Holy Sacraments.
The name of Jesus Christ: faith in Christ the Redeemer.

The preaching of Philip the deacon about Christ and the Kingdom of God made them believe in God and be baptized. Thus the Church of Samaria was founded, which was later known by the name of the Church of "Sebastia," from which came the Forty Martyrs mentioned in the Synaxarium and the Synod.

Simon then believed with a false faith, seeking benefit from the new situation, to get the chance to enter the Church and fight it from within after learning how to work miracles, thinking that the Apostles were sorcerers like himself. For this reason he stayed close to Philip and was astonished that he could not learn the making of the miracles, which he thought to be a kind of sorcery. His wickedness appeared afterward (vv. 18-23).

The response of the Apostles in Jerusalem to the news of the founding of the Church of Samaria was to send two close friends, Peter and John, who went down from Jerusalem, built on the mountains, to Samaria in the north to declare the Church's acceptance of the Samaritans into her fellowship, and the rejection of the Jewish fanaticism that forbids mingling with the Samaritans, and also to support the preaching in Samaria, and so that they might complete the grace for the believers by granting them the Holy Spirit. So they prayed with their apostolic authority for the descent of the Holy Spirit on the new believers. Here we see the greatness of the sacrament of the priesthood, for it is the right of the bishops, like the Apostles, to bestow the Holy Spirit on the baptized, by laying their hands on the baptized or by the priests anointing them with the oil of the Holy Myron.

Because of the small number of bishops and priests in the apostolic age, deacons such as Philip were permitted to baptize, but they have no authority to give the Holy Spirit in the sacrament of the Myron. So when Peter and John came, they prayed and laid their hands on the baptized and they received the Holy Spirit, that is, the sacrament of the Myron. Note here that the laying on of hands, which the Church received from the Church of the Old Testament, was a churchly delivery to show the authority of the priesthood.

The power: that is, the giving of the Holy Spirit, which was the right of the Apostles, so that if Simon were given the Holy Spirit, including the working of miracles, he would have a greater standing in the eyes of the people. Simon thought that the transfer of this authority to him was possible by bribery and paying the right price, so he offered a sum of money to the two Apostles, asking for this authority.
The Apostle Peter was angry and refused Simon's money, because the Holy Spirit does not come in return for a sum of money, and this thinking leads to destruction.
You have neither part: you will not receive the descent of the Holy Spirit or His gifts.
This matter: that is, the descent of the Holy Spirit upon him.

Not right: you do not believe in Christ out of love for Him and do not want to walk a spiritual walk, but you are still attached to money and position and want to use Christianity and the work of the Holy Spirit to achieve your purposes. Peter recalled, as a Jew, what Joshua did when he distributed the portions of the Promised Land among the tribes of old, so he declared to Simon that the crookedness of his heart had removed from him his share in the promise of the New Testament and the inheritance of the Kingdom, so his Christianity is rejected.
The bond of this: bribery to acquire the gifts of God with money.
Pray God: prayer is accepted from the repentant, so repentance is necessary first. If perhaps: if your repentance is sincere, you receive forgiveness, otherwise you will not receive it.
Peter called Simon to repent of this perverse thought and to pray to God, who could forgive him if his repentance was sincere.
The gall of bitterness: it means the severity of the sin into which Simon had fallen, which makes his life very bitter.
The bond of iniquity: a figure of his slavery to sin, by which he wrongs himself and leads others astray and wrongs them.

Pray ye: Simon was afraid at the words of the two Apostles, and even felt that his prayer was not accepted as a result of his falling into sin, so he asked for their prayer on his behalf, and this means two things:
1- His heart was not moved by repentance and love of God.
2- The importance of intercession in the prayers of others for them.
None of these things which ye have spoken: the destruction and eternal torment that the two Apostles warned him against reaching as a result of his wickedness.
Testified and preached: they completed the preaching and teaching of the Christian faith and the details of worship and spiritual conduct.

Preached in many villages: the ministry of the two Apostles was not limited to the city of Samaria, but they preached in many villages of the Samaritans, and this shows the importance of serving rich and poor, and also shows concern for every person. The two Apostles returned to Jerusalem, preaching in the villages on their way back.

Among the most dangerous things is trafficking in religion, a man's seeking religiosity not out of love for God but to gain a private benefit, the thing into which Judas fell when he finally sold his Master, and as Simon did, so that everyone who traffics in religion is called a simoniac.
Examine yourself, my brother: do you come to church and serve God out of love for Him, or do you have other purposes???
Do not lose your eternity for the sake of passing material things.

entries.section: (3) Philip the deacon and the eunuch

paragraphs.text: Down: because Jerusalem is built on the mountain.
Which is desert: that is, the desert road surrounded by wilderness.

God inspired an angel to speak to Philip and call him to go south to the desert road that descends from Jerusalem to Gaza, which is about a hundred kilometers long, running from Jerusalem westward to the Palestinian city of Gaza.

entries.section: (3) Philip the deacon and the eunuch

paragraphs.text: When Philip obeyed and went south and then west, he found an Ethiopian man, a proselyte to Judaism, who was a minister of the queen of Ethiopia, who was entitled Candace, a title like "Pharaoh" in Egypt and not a name, and he was in charge of the treasuries of the kingdom. We note that Solomon the Wise had a relation with Ethiopia since the queen of Sheba visited him. From that time there was a large Jewish community in Ethiopia, as there was in Alexandria.

entries.section: (3) Philip the deacon and the eunuch

paragraphs.text: After performing worship in Jerusalem, the eunuch was returning to his country, riding in his chariot and reading the Book of Isaiah, and this shows his devotion in his care to read the Holy Scriptures and not any trivial readings or yielding to laziness and ease.

entries.section: (3) Philip the deacon and the eunuch

paragraphs.text: Go near: walk beside the chariot.
Ran thither to him: he greeted the eunuch and spoke with him as a traveler on the same road, but on foot.

The Holy Spirit asked Philip to go forward to meet the minister, and this confirms for us the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit, for He is a hypostasis and not merely the power of God in the general sense.

entries.section: (3) Philip the deacon and the eunuch

paragraphs.text: Ran: Philip began the conversation with the eunuch.
Heard him read: the eunuch was reading aloud, and this helps many to concentrate on what they read.
He desired Philip: it appeared from Philip's words that he understood the words of Isaiah, so the eunuch seized the opportunity and asked him to ride with him and explain to him.
Philip asked him how well he understood what he was reading, and the man answered with great humility, asking for guidance and help, and invited Philip to get in and sit with him.

entries.section: (3) Philip the deacon and the eunuch

paragraphs.text: Opened not his mouth: Christ gave His life Himself for the redemption of mankind, so He did not defend Himself against the charges directed at Him, like sheep led to the slaughter, silent.
In his humiliation: He bore in humility all the sufferings, insults and injustice.
His judgment was taken away: the chief priests obtained an unjust sentence against Christ from the judging authority, that is, Pilate.
His generation: those contemporary with Christ.

Who shall declare: none of His contemporaries understands that He suffers for mankind and not for an evil He has done. His life is taken: He is sentenced to death on earth, but He is alive as God, so He rises again.

The eunuch was reading in Isaiah (Isa 53:7, 8), where he describes a person led to death while silent like a sheep or ewe at its slaughter or shearing, who in humility bore an unjust sentence that the wicked took from the judging authority, and killed Him. And the Jews of His generation did not understand that He suffered and died for others and not for a fault He had committed.
Then the eunuch asked Philip for the interpretation of these verses, and about the person of whom they speak... is it Isaiah or someone else?

entries.section: (3) Philip the deacon and the eunuch

paragraphs.text: Philip began to explain to the eunuch the story of the life of Christ and His redemption, and how these verses apply to Him, and how the Church began, and the joining of the believers by Baptism and the descent of the Holy Spirit upon them.

entries.section: (3) Philip the deacon and the eunuch

paragraphs.text: When they came to a pool of water, the eunuch asked Philip whether there was anything to prevent his being baptized. This confirms two things:

The first: that Baptism was performed only with much water, that is, by immersion, for if it were done by sprinkling he would have used the water he had with him, since a traveler in the desert must have drinking water with him. The second thing is that Philip spoke to him about Baptism and its importance after the acceptance of the faith.

entries.section: (3) Philip the deacon and the eunuch

paragraphs.text: I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God: he declared a brief faith in Christ the Savior and in His divinity. Philip made sure of the minister's faith in order to fulfill the Lord's commandment that "he that believeth and is baptized shall be saved" (Mk 16:16). This of course applies to adults, but as for children, their Christian parents can answer for them in the confession of faith until they grow up, so that they do not lose the blessing of the renewal of their nature and Communion from the Holy Mysteries merely because they are children.

entries.section: (3) Philip the deacon and the eunuch

paragraphs.text: They went down both into the water: Philip and the eunuch went down from the chariot to the pool of water that was beside the desert road, and the man was baptized by the hand of Philip.

entries.section: (3) Philip the deacon and the eunuch

paragraphs.text: Were come up: this shows that it was a collection of water into which the eunuch went down and immersed, and so was baptized by the hand of Philip. Caught away: the Holy Spirit suddenly transported him from this place to the city of Azotus to complete his work of preaching in it.
Rejoicing: in his faith and his Baptism, longing to preach this faith to his country.
The Holy Spirit transported Philip to the city of Azotus, so the minister no longer saw him, but went on his way rejoicing in his new faith.

entries.section: (3) Philip the deacon and the eunuch

paragraphs.text: Azotus: a Palestinian city lying north of Gaza at a distance of 24 miles.
Caesarea: named after Caesar, it is a great city on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea south of Acre.

Philip began to resume the preaching in the Palestinian city of Azotus until he reached Caesarea, from which afterward came the father of church history, the historian Bishop Eusebius of Caesarea, and in which a theological school was founded with scholars represented by the scholar Origen, who founded this school after he moved to it from Alexandria, and which was the dwelling place of Philip the deacon and his virgin daughters who prophesied (ch. 21:8, 9). Such was the activity of the first Church, which was restless in its work, but always moved to complete the mission under the guidance of the Holy Spirit and in obedience to Him.
May we move to serve God, and come out of our many occupations so that we may draw souls to enjoy fellowship with Him in the Church.
The conversion of Paul and the miracles of Peter

Breathing out threatenings: threatening and menacing, with his mouth uttering evil words full of hatred and vengeance. After the killing of Stephen, Saul was still very zealous for the destruction of Christianity, so he was threatening and killing many, trying to obtain from the high priest sentences of death against the Christians, who were called disciples.
Damascus: an ancient city lying north of Jerusalem at a distance of about 280 km, that is, a seven days' journey from it.
The synagogues: the communities of Jews present in no small number in Damascus.

The Way: the followers of the way of Christ, for so the Christians were called in the apostolic age, and he expected some of them to be in Damascus, of those who had been scattered by the Jewish persecution in Jerusalem.

Women: his cruelty appears in that he binds and drives not only men but women also. Saul asked the high priest to give him letters to the governor of Damascus and the elders of the Jewish communities, who had a large colony in Damascus, so that he might seize the Christians, men or women, with full force and transfer them in chains to be tried and tortured in Jerusalem.
While Paul was on the road near Damascus at noon (ch. 26:13), a heavenly light suddenly flashed around him, brighter than the light of the noonday sun.

In his great terror, he fell to the ground and saw the person of the Lord Jesus Christ, who spoke with him rebuking him and warning him of his persecution of the Christians, which Christ regarded as persecution of Himself personally. His rebuke of him was in humility and gentleness, as though asking the reason for that persecution, for the Lord and His Church are in union like the head and the body. The speech was in the Hebrew language, and those with him did not understand the words although they heard the voice (ch. 26:14).
Pricks: plural of goad, which is an iron needle that the farmer uses to prick the animal so that it hurries on its way and work.

Saul asked who was speaking, and God made clear to him that He is Jesus, which is His name according to the flesh, to make clear to him that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and in compassion for him made him understand that he would harm no one but himself, because all the sorrows of the Church are turned into blessings and joys and the harm falls on its persecutors and not on it, like one who kicks with his foot iron needles, which are the goads, so his foot is wounded and the blood flows from it, while the goads suffer no harm.

Saul was greatly bewildered because he was surprised by a divine proclamation of the divinity of Jesus, and was terrified when he sensed the greatness of the wrong he had been committing during his persecution of the Church, and in submission he asked for God's counsel in order to carry it out, so God directed him to enter Damascus, where he would be told what was required of him.

Thus God made clear the necessity of submitting to the Church and her priests, to receive the Holy Sacraments from their hand and to hear the teachings and guidance, for a man cannot be content with his personal relationship with God apart from the Church, or with hearing the voice of God and the guidance of the Spirit without the guidance of the Church.
All who were with him were silent with terror, not understanding the words although they heard the voice, and they did not see the person of the Lord but saw only the light.

He saw no man: because he had seen Christ in His strong light, whereas those with him saw something of the light and did not see Christ, so they did not lose their sight. This was by God's permission that he might be humbled, for humility is the entrance to the spiritual life.

Saul arose after losing his sight temporarily from the intensity of the light, so he could no longer see anyone. Thus for one who sees the Lord, the sight of anyone else becomes small. They led him by the hand, and he entered Damascus not in the manner he had wanted, not in a grand procession but in humility and reverence.
Saul remained for three days in fasting, constant prayers and meditation on what had happened, seeing nothing throughout this time.
So the Lord intervenes in His love in our lives to change our course at the right moment, and therefore we must be discerning of His voice and obedient to Him.

entries.section: (2) Faith, Baptism and the beginning of ministry

paragraphs.text: A disciple: that is, a Christian.
A vision: a sight he saw while awake and not in a dream.
Of Tarsus: from Tarsus, the capital of Cilicia in Asia Minor (present-day Turkey), a great city famous for learning.
He prayeth: his prayers now are in humility and different from his former prayers as a Pharisee in pride.

He hath seen in a vision: Saul was awake, and although he could not see the material things around him, God revealed to him a spiritual sight, which was that a priest named Ananias entered to him and put his hands on his eyes and he saw. The Lord appeared to one of the Christians of Damascus, whose name was Ananias, and he was a priest because he baptized Saul afterward, and the Lord said to him in the vision to go to the main street in Damascus, which was called Straight Street, and was the longest street in the city, running from east to west, four meters wide and lined by rows of columns, and it still exists today. And He asked him to go to the house of a man named Judas, where he would find Saul of Tarsus praying, and the Lord informed him that Saul had seen him, that is, had seen Ananias in a vision, putting his hands on Saul's eyes so that he might see. Thus God gave clear signs to Ananias and to Saul to reassure them.

entries.section: (2) Faith, Baptism and the beginning of ministry

paragraphs.text: Ananias was bewildered when he heard God's words in the vision about going to Saul, because he had heard from the Christians of Jerusalem who had fled to Damascus of Saul's wickedness and his persecution of the believers, and that he had come to Damascus with authority from the high priest to seize the Christians, torture them and kill them, but in spite of that he was ready to obey God, for he declared his submission at the beginning of the vision by saying, "Behold, I am here, Lord."

entries.section: (2) Faith, Baptism and the beginning of ministry

paragraphs.text: Gentiles: he will preach to non-Jews, and this was something far from the understanding of the Jews, for they thought that they alone were the people of God, and none other would believe in the Messiah.
Kings: he means the rulers, of kings and governors, who tried the Apostle Paul, and he even preached Christ to some of them, such as Felix, Festus, Agrippa and Nero.

The children of Israel: Paul preached, at the beginning of his entering any country, to the Jews first and then to the Gentiles in it. God reassured Ananias to go to Paul, since He had chosen him as a vessel to fill, to proclaim His name to many Gentiles and kings and to the people of the children of Israel; a thing that was perfectly fulfilled in Paul's preaching in the future, and He also informed him that he would suffer much for the sake of Christ, and that is something every Christian goes through.

entries.section: (2) Faith, Baptism and the beginning of ministry

paragraphs.text: Ananias was reassured and went to the house of Judas, and blessed Saul by putting his hands on him for blessing and not for ordination, and called him brother in gentleness and love despite all he had done before, and told him that Christ had sent him to him after appearing to him on the road to Damascus, to restore to him sight and insight by faith and to be filled with the Holy Spirit after Baptism.

entries.section: (2) Faith, Baptism and the beginning of ministry

paragraphs.text: Scales fell from Saul's eyes to confirm God's miracle, and these scales are a symbol of the sin that had veiled Christ from him, so he received sight immediately and Ananias baptized him.

entries.section: (2) Faith, Baptism and the beginning of ministry

paragraphs.text: Saul took food and was strengthened after his fast of three days, and stayed some days with the Christians of Damascus. Thus the wolf was turned into a lamb.

entries.section: (2) Faith, Baptism and the beginning of ministry

paragraphs.text: Straightway: immediately after his Baptism.

He preached: his preaching includes that after his Baptism and also after his return from his retreat in the Arabian desert. The synagogues: the Apostles used to enter them as Jews and then preach Christ, confirming their words from the prophecies of the prophets.

The Church began her ministry as a daughter of the Jewish nation and emerging from it, which helped the spread of Christianity among the Jews. And Saul began to preach in the synagogues of the Jews in the name of Christ and His divinity; but we must know that after his Baptism he went to the Arabian desert bordering Damascus, where he stayed three years in retreat in which Christ appeared to him, and delivered to him the faith and the Holy Sacraments (Gal 1:16-18), so some of the Fathers call him the thirteenth of the Apostles, and then he returned to Damascus for ministry.

entries.section: (2) Faith, Baptism and the beginning of ministry

paragraphs.text: Saul's ministry was met with great astonishment by the Jews, who knew his past in Jerusalem in opposing the Christians, whom he had now joined, having come to torture them.

entries.section: (2) Faith, Baptism and the beginning of ministry

paragraphs.text: The Jews wondered greatly at his power of persuasion as a student of the Law and the Prophets, proving that Jesus is the Christ.
Truly nothing is too hard for the Lord!.. Who would have thought that such a complete change would happen?!
He who changed Saul, which means (the asked-for one), into Paul, which means (the little one), still asks us to allow Him to change our lives into true children of His.

God is able to change you whatever your sins or weaknesses, for He is your Creator who loves you and is able to do all things, but it remains that you do not reject the voice of God within you or when you hear it from the Church and her servants. Do not resist the word of God or wallow in your sins, but rise up, confident of His support for you, and you will gain your life and become great like Paul.

After Saul completed three years in the desert called Arabia, he returned to Damascus, and the Jews were greatly distressed by his preaching, so they took counsel to kill him as they had done with Stephen.
Saul learned of their plot, for the Jews had agreed with the governor of the city to seize him, so they watched the gates of the city to seize him when he came out of one of them.

The believers, the disciples of Christ, took him to the house of one of them that adjoined the wall of the city, where they let him down from it in a large basket so that he could get out without the Jews seeing him. The decision was based on Christ's words to His disciples: "When they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another" (Mt 10:23), so that the preaching might spread.

Thus Paul escaped from the plot of the Jews and left Damascus as a fugitive, contrary to what he had expected when he came to the city to seize the Christians in it and go out in pride dragging many of them to be tortured and killed in Jerusalem.

Saul arrived from Damascus in Jerusalem and tried to join the Christians there, but they were afraid of him, thinking he was a spy for the Jews, especially because of the long period of his disappearance in the Arabian desert, which made them suspect that he had returned to his Judaism.

Barnabas: one of the first disciples who followed Christ with the twelve, and he was rich and sold his field and gave it to the Apostles for the needs of the believers (Acts 4:36, 37). He was of the tribe of Levi and had lived before in Cyprus, so he was Cypriot by nationality.

Barnabas intervened and brought him to Peter and James (Gal 1:18, 19), the two Apostles who were still in Jerusalem, because the rest were traveling to preach, and told them of the sincerity of his faith and Christ's appearing to him on the road to Damascus and his ministry in it.
At last the Christians of Jerusalem were reassured about him, and he began his preaching there, but for about fifteen days only (Gal 1:18).

Saul began to persuade the Greek-speaking Jews in the synagogues where Stephen had addressed them, so they also tried to kill him, and the Christians sent him to the city of Caesarea, which lies between Acre and Joppa, and God had also commanded him to leave Jerusalem (ch. 22:17-21), and then he traveled from Caesarea to Tarsus by sea and stayed there about three or four years.

Be strong in proclaiming the truth however much others oppose you or you are exposed to trouble, confident that God keeps you to proclaim His name, and at the same time do not waste your time in clashing with others but flee from evil to continue your positive work in calling everyone to life with God.

Had rest: the Jewish persecution of the Church subsided because many Christians had been scattered in the countries of the world and left Jerusalem, in addition to the change of the greatest opponent of the Christians, Saul of Tarsus, who became a Christian and a preacher of Christ, and finally because the Jews were occupied with the conflict with the Roman authority.
The fear of the Lord: it gave the believers piety and a spiritual walk, which drew many to faith.
The comfort of the Holy Ghost: that is, His encouragements and His support for the children of God.

The Church extended from Jerusalem to Judea and then Samaria and Galilee, that is, all the parts of the land of the Jews; and the Jews' persecution of the Christians subsided after their killing of Stephen, because the Jews were occupied with their problems with the Emperor "Caligula," who ordered that a statue of himself be set up in the Temple, so the whole country was in uproar and the governor advised him to postpone this matter. Thus the Jews forgot the Church in the midst of their problems, and the Church grew and multiplied in the fear of God and the comfort of the Comforter Spirit.
Lydda: a city lying east of Joppa at a distance of 9 miles.

The Apostle Peter began a visiting tour, and came down to the believers at Lydda. We note that he was visiting only those who had turned to Christianity from the Jews, because the faith had not yet spread among the Gentiles. We see here a new name for the Christians, who were called first disciples, then believers, then saints, then brethren and finally Christians.

There was in Lydda a Christian, sick with paralysis for eight years and known to all, named Aeneas, and Peter healed him in the name of Jesus Christ and commanded him to rise and make his bed himself, and he arose immediately.
Sharon: it is the fertile plain extending from Joppa to Caesarea.
All who dwelt at Lydda and Sharon, of the believers, saw him, and the miracle was a cause of the strengthening of their faith.

"To every purpose under heaven there is a time" (Eccl 3:1), and the Lord is able to stretch out the hand of healing at the right time. So let us not despair if the trial or illness is prolonged, but let us benefit from it in strengthening our relationship with God, confident of His power and wisdom, which chooses the right time.
Joppa: a port on the Mediterranean Sea thirty miles south of Caesarea and 45 miles west of Jerusalem, and it is the most important port in Judea.
A disciple: a Christian woman.
There lived at Joppa a Christian woman named Tabitha, which is a Syriac name meaning gazelle, and she was righteous and charitable.

Tabitha fell sick and died, and they washed her, for it is the custom of Christians to wash the body after death (as a symbol of purity and cleanness, but it is merely a custom and not a necessary thing), and they did not bury her but sent two men to call Peter from Lydda to Joppa (15 km) to attend the funeral and console the believers, and asked him to come quickly so that the burial would not be delayed. Perhaps they had hope of her being raised from the dead.

Peter came quickly and went up with those gathered to the upper room where the body was, and the widows showed him, weeping, the garments that Tabitha used to make for the brethren of the Lord, and Peter was deeply moved.
Sat up: a proclamation of her life after having been dead.
Gave her his hand: so that she would be sure that she was alive and lean on his hand and rise and go out to those gathered. The saints: the believers sanctified in Christ.

Peter put everyone out of the room so that he might pray to the Lord to raise her, so that no one would see him doing that, because he does not seek fame or greatness, and he asked Christ to raise her and she sat up at once and He restored her alive.
Tarried: he settled in Joppa to complete his preaching of Christ.
Many days: about three years.
After that Peter stayed a long time in Joppa in the house of Simon the tanner.

Truly "almsgiving delivers from death," as the Scripture says (Tob 4:7). May you love giving because it is a great blessing, and know that when you give to one in need you are offering love to Christ Himself. So do not be lax in helping all those around you even by a small deed or kind words, and if you are unable to act and speak, your prayer moves God's mercies, so that He cares for them.
The acceptance of the Gentiles into the faith
Caesarea: the main Roman military base in the land of Palestine, about 30 miles from Joppa; this distance requires a day and a half of travel on foot.

Band: the Roman army had many bands from all nations, but the Italian band was the best of them, because its members were from Italy, that is, Roman by origin. Each band consisted of 400 to 600 soldiers.
Cornelius: his name in Greek means “like a horn,” that is, strong. He was one of the officers of this distinguished Italian band.

Cornelius, his whole family and those who served him were Gentiles, that is, non-Jews, but they feared God and revered Him, and they prayed to Him and gave alms and acts of kindness to the Jews who were under their authority in Caesarea. Five virtues appear in Cornelius from this:
A devout man: he lives in righteousness and goodness and obeys God.
One who feared God: he is concerned to please God and to keep away from sin.
With all his house: he is concerned for the spiritual life of the members of his household, whether his relatives or his servants.

Gave much alms: he was concerned to show kindness to the poor and needy, although he was a Roman, and he did not act like the rest of the Romans in violence and oppression toward the inhabitants of the lands they occupy, such as the Jews. Prayed to God: although he was a pagan, he seems to have been influenced by what he had heard about the God of Israel, so he worshiped the God whom he did not know and prayed to Him, and even persevered in prayer night and day.
While Cornelius was awake at about the ninth hour of the day, perhaps while he was praying, he saw an angel coming in to him and calling him by name in order to reassure him.
Looked on him: he gazed with attention and wonder.
He was afraid: because of the majesty of the angel’s radiant appearance.
What is it, Lord?: here the humility of Cornelius and his submission to God and His angels appear.
For a memorial before God: that is, God remembered them, accepted them and rejoiced in them.

Cornelius spoke with the angel in fear and asked him what he wanted him to do, and the angel answered him that his prayers and good works had been accepted by God as a sweet fragrance like sacrifices, so the Lord remembered him for good.
Simon: his name before he became a disciple of Christ.
Whose surname is Peter: the name that Christ gave him.

By the sea side: perhaps the reason is the work of tanning, which needs much water, so he lived beside the sea; and the angel’s purpose in saying this was to specify exactly the house of Simon so that Peter could be reached easily. What thou oughtest to do: the foundations of the right faith and sound worship.

Because the salvation of man requires faith, Baptism, good works, the sacraments and so on, the angel asked Cornelius to summon the Apostle Peter from Joppa, where he was staying after the raising of Tabitha, in the house of Simon the tanner; and although Philip the Evangelist was living in Caesarea, the Lord commanded that Peter be summoned.

Here we see the Lord’s respect for the priesthood, and therefore the angel did not take Peter’s place in preaching to Cornelius. Thus, just as Peter began to preach to the Jews on the day of Pentecost, he began to preach to the Gentiles with Cornelius.
When he was departed: immediately after the angel disappeared, Cornelius called his men to carry out the word of God, so his obedience was swift.
A devout soldier: the devout life of Cornelius influenced not only his house but also his work, so that some of his soldiers became devout like this soldier.
Waited on him continually: Cornelius used to draw near to himself the devout among his servants and soldiers, encouraging them and being encouraged by them on the way of the spiritual life.
All these things: the details of the vision.

Cornelius sent a group of his men whom he trusted, and explained to them what had happened, asking them to summon Peter from Joppa. Thus we see Cornelius’s immediate obedience to God’s call, which we need to imitate in our conduct.

Be confident that your worship and the good works you do reach God and He values them greatly, and because of them God pours out His blessings upon you, for your worship and service declare your love and longing toward God. So continue your prayers, your alms and your love for everyone, for they are the proof of your sonship to God.
Journeyed, and drew nigh unto the city: between Joppa and Caesarea is about 30 miles, so it requires a journey of about 12 hours.
The housetop: a quiet place, apart from the noise of the house, suited to praying in stillness.

The sixth hour: the Jews prayed at the third and the ninth hours, and the devout among them added prayer at the sixth hour as well, which is twelve noon by present reckoning. The journey took up the rest of the day on which the angel appeared and all of the second day until noon, and on that day the Apostle Peter was praying on the housetop of the house of Simon the tanner in Joppa at about twelve noon, according to the custom of the Jews.
Fell upon him: God caused him to sleep and to lose consciousness.
Peter was fasting, so after the prayer he became hungry and asked for food, and while they were preparing it for him he lost consciousness; for prayer helps in the revealing of the divine will.
Heaven opened: that is, split open, and the sheet came down from it.
A great sheet: a very large sheet let down and bound at its four corners, so that it was in the shape of a huge vessel.
All manner of fourfooted beasts of the earth: this includes all kinds of animals that God created.
A voice: from heaven, that is, from God.

Peter saw a sheet coming down from heaven, and this signifies that it was a heavenly revelation. God made use of his hunger to reveal to him, through food, an important idea: that God longs for the salvation of all the nations and not only the Jews, as they supposed. In the sheet were all kinds of animals, some of which the Jewish Law considered unclean (Lev 11:2-7; Deut 14:3-20). And he heard a voice from heaven commanding him to eat of them.
Not so, Lord: this is not an objection to God but astonishment, because it contradicts the Law of Moses, which divides animals into clean and unclean and commands not to eat the latter.

Common or unclean: according to the Law of Moses, which was a symbol of keeping away from uncleanness; but in the New Testament “unto the pure all things are pure” (Titus 1:15). Peter, as a Jew, was astonished at the divine command, because the Jews do not eat forbidden foods.

A voice again: the first time He said to him, “Rise, kill, and eat,” and the second time it was a confirmation that all animals are clean because they are God’s creation, and all the more so all human beings because they are His image; and whoever believes is cleansed by the blood of Christ, whether Jew or Gentile.

The voice made him know that God had cleansed the whole world and that there was no longer any unclean food, as an indication that the Gentiles were no longer unclean, because the blood of Christ is sufficient to cleanse whoever believes in Him and walks in the way of salvation.

Thrice: after the likeness of the Holy Trinity, to confirm the idea of the acceptance of the Gentiles. The voice was repeated three times, then the whole was taken up into heaven from which it had come down, as an indication that the vision was real, to convey a message, and not merely a scene that vanishes.

This divine command is not an abolition of the Law but a fulfillment of it, since the redemption of Christ was no longer hidden from the Gentiles so that they should be called unclean, as the Jews supposed.
Christ has cleansed us as Gentiles and opened to us the door of salvation, which we must live and enjoy with all our feelings.
Have a heart open in love to everyone, confident that God seeks the salvation of all; even those who appear far off and wicked may believe and come to God and precede you into the Kingdom.
Doubted in himself: perplexed, what is the meaning of the vision?

While Peter was thinking about the meaning of the vision, whether God meant that all foods are blessed and permitted or whether there was another meaning, behold, the messengers of Cornelius arrived at the house where Peter was staying and asked for him.
Three men: this was a sign given by the Spirit to Peter, who did not know who was at the door, so that he might be assured that God had sent them and wanted him to go with them.
Nothing doubting: because they were Gentiles.
While Peter was thinking about the vision, the Holy Spirit alerted him to the arrival of the men who were seeking him and commanded him to go with them in assurance.
Went down: from the housetop to the door of the house.
From Cornelius: this is the word of Luke, because Peter did not know the men.

What is the cause: the Holy Spirit did not reveal the cause to him, so that he would take it upon himself to ask the men and they would explain to him, and love and friendship would be established between them.
Peter obeyed and presented himself to the men and asked them the reason for their coming.
A centurion: one of the commanders of the Roman army who were spread throughout Judea because they occupied it. A holy angel: to distinguish him from the fallen angels, that is, the demons.

The men told Peter about Cornelius, who was known among the Jews for his righteousness, and that an angel had appeared to him to summon Peter, in order to explain why Cornelius had not come to Peter himself, for these were the angel’s orders that Peter should go to him, and this, as we will understand later, was so that the preaching to the Gentiles might begin.

Peter hosted them until the next day so that they might begin the journey back after resting that day, and Peter took with him some believing men from Joppa to be witnesses of what would happen, namely the acceptance of the Gentiles.

The servant must obey God and not seek what is for himself, however strange the divine word may be to his mind or however difficult the commandments, for God will give help to carry them out and will explain to him afterward the power and blessing of the divine commandments.
Do not neglect the guidance of your father of confession even if it is against your desires, and be confident that you will receive abundant blessings of obedience.

On the day after they set out from Joppa, they arrived at Cornelius in Caesarea, and Cornelius felt responsible toward his family and friends, so he summoned them to hear the good news of salvation. Thus the righteous man is a cause of blessing to those around him, just as the wicked man is a cause of harm to his companions.

When Peter arrived, Cornelius prostrated himself before him out of respect, but Peter feared that Cornelius’s pagan origin had made him think Peter was a god in the flesh, so he said to him, “Stand up,” and made clear to him that he was only a man, and continued speaking with him until the two entered the place where the brethren were gathered.

Unlawful: the teachings of the Jewish elders stipulated not mixing with the Gentiles, although the Law did not teach this and meant only not to share in their evils or to intermarry with them. God hath shewed me: through the sight of the sheet coming down from heaven.
Without gainsaying: without dispute or refusal.

I ask: although he had heard some information from the messengers of Cornelius, he wanted to hear from Cornelius himself, so that perhaps some details might appear and his answer would complete what Cornelius had seen, so that those present would be convinced and believe.

Peter informed them, without explaining the details of the vision, that although the scholars of the Jews warn a Jew against mixing with the Gentiles, God had commanded him to come and had convinced him of the cleanness of the Gentiles, so he came with all speed without objection, and asked them the reason for their summoning him.

Four days ago: the distance between Caesarea and Joppa takes about a day and a half going, then a day and a half returning, and so about four days had passed since the vision of Cornelius. This hour: at the ninth hour by Jewish reckoning, that is, three in the afternoon. Fasting: this shows the devotion of Cornelius, who joined his fasts with prayers, as if he were a Jew walking by the Law because he had been influenced by his Jewish fellow citizens.
A man: he means the angel.
In bright clothing: he was radiant and his appearance was glorious.
Is heard… are had in remembrance: God cares about the prayers and alms of His human children, and even if they do not know the faith, He guides them because of their love for Him.
Shall speak unto thee: he will explain to you the right faith.

Cornelius made clear to the Apostle Peter what the angel had done, who informed him that God had accepted his prayers and alms, and asked him to summon Peter from the house of Simon the tanner in Joppa so that he might speak with him.
Immediately: this shows Cornelius’s swift obedience to God.
Thou hast well done: thanks, praise and welcome to Peter.

Before God: this shows the submission of Cornelius and those with him to the words of Peter, which are God’s voice to them. Cornelius hastened and summoned Peter and thanked him for the speed of his coming, and asked him to begin his message with which God had sent him.

The Holy Spirit prepares the way of the servant and readies the heart of the one being served, so may we resort to Him in prayer in every service that God sets before us, confident in His power that works in us and opens hearts to us, however stubborn, resistant or distant they may be.
Peter opened his mouth: this shows the importance of the speech that Peter began, namely the preaching to the Gentiles and their acceptance into the faith.
Of a truth I perceive: through the revelation of the sheet coming down from heaven and the appearance of the angel to Cornelius, all this confirms God’s acceptance of the Gentiles into the faith.
No respecter of persons: He is not influenced by a person’s appearance or position, so He shows partiality to no one, but has mercy on everyone who takes refuge in Him with faith.
Peter began to preach, declaring that God does not favor one people over another.
Feareth him, and worketh righteousness: that is, he has a good conscience and obeys the voice of God in his conscience, so he keeps away from sin and does good works.

Accepted with him: God is pleased with this good disposition in him, so He reveals to him the good news of salvation that he may believe and become a member of His Church, as is proved by Peter’s preaching to the hearers and their Baptism. Of course it does not mean that he is accepted without joining the Church, because this is against all the teachings of the Holy Bible and against the rest of this sermon of Peter. This mistaken belief is called the heresy of “universal salvation,” that is, that every person is saved while remaining in his own religion and sect, and does not need faith in Christ or joining the Church and its sacraments and means of grace.
Peter made clear that God’s choice is not limited to the Jews, but whoever seeks Him finds Him.
The word: the Gospel that is preached to the Jews.
Peace: the goal of the preaching of the Gospel is reconciliation between man and God, and between the spirit and the body, so that he receives inner peace.
By Jesus Christ: the foundation of the preaching of the Gospel is the blood of Christ the Redeemer on the Cross, who is the head of the Church.
Lord of all: a declaration of the divinity of Christ, for He is the Lord of all humanity, Jews and Gentiles, and He came for the salvation of all.
That word: the preaching of Christ in Galilee and Judea.
The baptism which John preached: the preaching of Christ began after the completion of its preparation, namely the preaching of John the Baptist and his baptism.
Peter directed the attention of those gathered to the preaching of Christ, which He began after His baptism by John the Baptist.
Jesus of Nazareth: this shows His humanity and the homeland in which He lived most of His life, namely the city of Nazareth in Galilee.
God was with him: an indication of the divinity working in Him to heal the sick, cast out demons and perform all the miracles.

The Christ is Jesus of Nazareth, who was anointed with the Holy Spirit at His baptism as Christ and Savior of the world, and the Spirit gave Him all power, so He did all good and rescued many from the slavery of the devil, who had dominion over them through various diseases and troubles.

The Apostle Peter declares that he and the rest of the Apostles are witnesses of the teachings and miracles of Christ in Jerusalem and Judea, this One whom the Jews killed by crucifixion at the hands of the Romans.

God raised him up: as the humanity of Christ was declared in (v. 38), here He declares His divinity in that God raised Him up, that is, God united with the humanity in Christ raised Him up, that is, raised Himself from the dead. This expression was used so that people would not fall into a duality of divinity if he declared that Christ is God, lest some think that He is another god besides the God of the Old Testament known to the Jews; so he affirms here that He is one God who raised up Jesus Christ, that is, His divinity raised His humanity which is united with it.

After the resurrection of Christ from the dead He appeared openly, not to all the Jews who had rejected Him, but to those who believed in Him and whom He had chosen as disciples, and He ate and drank with them to confirm His resurrection to them.

Christ commanded His disciples, and those to whom He appeared after His resurrection, to preach what they had seen to the whole world, that they might believe and walk in a pure life, and to declare that He will come to judge the world at the end of the days, rewarding the righteous believers and punishing the wicked who refuse.
