The second journey and Paul’s preaching in Europe and Asia

The second journey was distinguished by the beginning of the preaching in Europe for the first time, in the city of Philippi. The journey went from Antioch (Syria) by land to Tarsus (Turkey), then by land to Derbe (Turkey), and after that by land to Lystra (Turkey), and from it by land to Iconium (Turkey), and after that by land to Troas (Turkey), then by sea to Neapolis (Europe), and from there he went by land to Philippi (Europe), and from it by land to Amphipolis (Europe), and after that by land to Apollonia (Europe), and from it he traveled by land to Thessalonica (Europe), and after that by land to Berea (Europe), followed by Athens (Europe) by land, and from there he moved to Cenchrea (Greece) by land, and after that to Corinth (Greece) also by land, and sailed from it to Ephesus (Turkey), then by sea to Caesarea (Palestine), and finally arrived at Jerusalem by land. The second journey is recorded from (ch. 15:36 to ch. 18:22), and it took the period from A.D. 51 to 54, that is, three and a half years.

In Lystra lived Timothy, who became a disciple of the Apostle Paul; his mother was called Eunice (that is, the victorious will), and his father was a pagan Greek. Everyone bore witness to Timothy’s faith, spirituality and service.

Paul wanted to take Timothy with him as a disciple on his journey to help him, as he had taken Mark before, so he circumcised him first so that he could preach with him in the synagogues of the Jews and they would not reject him because of his Greek origin.

The Apostles used to deliver the decisions of the Council of Jerusalem to every city they went to where they had founded churches, so that none of the Jewish converts would trouble them, but they would be confident that they did not need circumcision and the Law after their Baptism and joining the Church.
The churches were increasing in number and in strength in the faith as the days passed.
Phrygia: a large province in the middle of Asia Minor, that is, Turkey, west of Pisidia, and among its most important cities are Colossae, Hierapolis and Laodicea.
Galatia: a province in Asia Minor lying east of Phrygia, most of whose inhabitants were pagans, with some Jews among them.

Asia: a province in western Asia Minor, that is, Turkey, whose capital is Ephesus, and in it lie the seven cities to which the letters were sent in the Book of Revelation, and it is of course different from the continent of Asia. The Apostles passed through the middle of Turkey and Galatia, but the Holy Spirit forbade them to preach in Ephesus in western Turkey.
Mysia: a province in the northwest of Asia Minor.
Bithynia: a province in Asia Minor lying east of Mysia, whose capital is Nicaea, where the first Ecumenical Council met.
Troas: a port in the province of Mysia lying on the Mediterranean Sea.
In Mysia the Apostles wanted to go east to preach in Bithynia in Turkey, but the Holy Spirit directed them westward to cross the sea to Greece from the Turkish port of Troas.
A man of Macedonia: from Macedonia, which is the first province in Europe in Greece, from which Alexander the Great came out.
Come over… and help us: he calls him to preach in Europe to help them and bring them out of the darkness of paganism into the light of Christianity.
A vision appeared to Paul in the night calling him to cross from Turkey to Europe to preach in it.

Paul and his companions met Luke, who was preaching in Troas, and he joined them, and when the vision appeared to Paul, all of them moved by sea to Macedonia (Greece), being sure that God wanted them to preach in Europe.

Do not be troubled if some of your plan and arrangements are held up for reasons beyond your control, for God’s will is better than your will; only be faithful in what is in your hands and accept God’s arrangements, and be flexible and adapt to the new circumstances, confident that all things work together for good to them that love God.
Loosed: we traveled by sea, and this sea voyage took two days until we reached Neapolis.
Samothracia: a small island between Troas and Neapolis.
Neapolis: that is, the new city, and it is the port of the city of Philippi.
Paul and his companions moved from Troas in Asia to Samothracia by sea, then to Neapolis in Greece.
A colony: that is, a city that enjoys the same rights as Rome.

They left Neapolis, most likely because there were no Jews in it, and headed to Philippi in the province of Macedonia in northern Greece, which is a city whose inhabitant is a Roman citizen with the rights of the people of Rome, and they stayed in it for some days.

When the Sabbath came, Paul began the preaching at a gathering of the Jews that was held outside the city, which had no synagogue, and the Jews used to meet by the river because it was forbidden for a religion that was not recognized to enter Philippi, and also the river is suitable for getting water for purification. And they began to speak to the women who had gathered for prayer.

Purple: the color of a red dye extracted from shellfish, with which the fabrics worn by kings and the great were dyed, and Lydia sold this luxurious kind of cloth. Thyatira: a city in Asia Minor in which John the Beloved preached and which is mentioned in the Book of Revelation. One that worshipped God: a Gentile woman who was influenced by the Jews and loved the worship of God.
Lydia heard the Apostles, and she was a Gentile from Turkey, and she believed in Christ.
Ye have judged me to be faithful: you agreed to my faith, as proved by your baptizing me, so it becomes my right to receive the blessing of hosting you.

She constrained us: Paul and those with him were self-denying and did not want to burden anyone, and they ate from the work of their hands, but the virtue of hospitality to strangers appears in Lydia, who urged them to be her guests. After the Baptism of Lydia and her household, which confirms the Baptism of children, she hosted them in her house.

Care for the strangers in your church or your place of residence or work, encouraging them with your kind words and helping them as much as you can. Put yourself in their place to feel for them, and know that this love of yours is offered to God Himself, for Christ said that whoever hosts a stranger has as it were hosted Him, and Abraham, when he hosted strangers, discovered that he had hosted God and His angels.

entries.section: (3) The damsel with the spirit of divination

paragraphs.text: Her masters: her lords who used her for knowledge of the unseen in order to profit from this work, and they were a large number since she brought them much money.

On their way in the morning to the prayer of the third hour, which is the first of the Jews’ prayers, that is, nine in the morning by present reckoning, and perhaps the place is the one mentioned in (v. 13), there was a damsel possessed with a demon who worked as a diviner, that is, she disclosed some near future matters, which are events that Satan had seen and that had taken place in distant places and had not yet reached man, and she brought her masters great gain.

entries.section: (3) The damsel with the spirit of divination

paragraphs.text: Followed: she listened to Paul’s preaching and continued to follow him in his movements, because Satan wants to know the words of the preaching in order to oppose it.

Cried: it was the custom of some diviners at that time to cry out to draw people’s attention and then announce the unseen things, so here she cried out as was her custom to declare the fact that Paul and those with him are servants of God. The diviner followed Paul and his companions, and Satan went on disturbing them so that people would not hear their preaching. And Satan bore witness to Paul and those with him, to win the confidence of the crowds who follow Paul, so that he might go on leading them astray.

entries.section: (3) The damsel with the spirit of divination

paragraphs.text: Being grieved: because of the disturbance she was causing, and out of pity for her as a person tormented by Satan, and so that Satan would not win the people’s favor and trust by his testimony.
The same hour: that is, immediately.

When the diviner had done this for many days, Paul was troubled, because Satan’s testimony to Christ is rejected, and he commanded the spirit in the name of Christ to come out of her, and it came out immediately.

The testimony of the wicked is not accepted because of their bad conduct. So be careful in your behavior and your speech lest you cause anyone to stumble when you speak about God. Reject everything that does not befit you as a Christian even if it is not a sin, and repent quickly of your sins so that God will cover you and you will not cause anyone to stumble.
Saw: a calm appeared on the damsel which informed them that she had been delivered from Satan.
Caught Paul and Silas: because they were the ones who spoke and led, and they did not seize those with them, who were Luke and Timothy.
The marketplace: where people gather and trials are held.
As a result of the stopping of the profit of the owners of the damsel, they dragged Paul and Silas to the rulers of the city.
The magistrates: the Roman military rulers, because it is a city subject to the Roman authority. Do exceedingly trouble: they stir up anxiety and disturbance in the city.
Being Jews: they mentioned their nationality because the Jews are hated by the Roman authority.

Customs: it was not permitted in the Roman system to practice any new religion or customs except with permission of the authority, so the masters showed that these customs are foreign to the Roman way of thinking and not approved by the authority.
The masters of the damsel made accusations against Paul and Silas that merit death, namely preaching a strange doctrine in a Roman city, which causes confusion in the city and its disturbance.

The multitude rose up: the masters of the damsel were able to stir up the people because they had lost the one who told them the unseen in their private problems, and because Paul and Silas were Jews, their customs and teachings were against the Romans.

The magistrates had Paul and Silas stripped to flog them with unusual violence, tearing their clothes instead of removing them, and commanded that they be beaten with rods on their backs with unaccustomed cruelty (2 Cor 11:25), and they charged the keeper of the prison to tighten the guard over them as being among the worst criminals who need more than the ordinary guarding.

The stocks: a wooden device to fasten the head, hands and feet of the guilty man in its five openings, so that he cannot move and remains in a position painful to his whole body, as he lies on his back.

The jailer put Paul and Silas in the deepest place in the prison, which is the inner prison, which usually no light or air enters but which is like a cave beneath the ordinary prison, and only one who is awaiting death is imprisoned in it, and he fastened their feet in the stocks, and their backs were bloody from the effect of the severe beating with rods.

Endure sufferings for the sake of holding fast to God’s commandments or serving Him, however severe the tribulations, for God will support you; He permits Satan to show all his evil and then is glorified in you and gives you victory. And know that everything you endure is very precious in God’s eyes and He will reward you for it, not only in this life but rather in eternal life.

entries.section: (5) The opening of the prison and the faith of the jailer

paragraphs.text: At midnight: the pain kept them from sleeping, and this helped them to pray and praise.
Prayed and sang praises: since they rejoiced to share with Christ in His sufferings.

Paul and Silas went on praying at midnight with a wonderful, constant joy, making light of the fetters and the pain, and the prisoners listened to them instead of sleeping because of the strangeness of the matter.

entries.section: (5) The opening of the prison and the faith of the jailer

paragraphs.text: A great earthquake: a mighty declaration of the power of God to whom Paul and Silas pray, and the prisoners heard them and understood that the earthquake was connected with their prayer, and that they were the cause of the opening of the doors and the loosing of the fetters; and from the horror of the surprise none of the prisoners moved from his place despite there being ample opportunity to escape.

entries.section: (5) The opening of the prison and the faith of the jailer

paragraphs.text: Awaking out of his sleep: the jailer had fallen asleep, and this is a fault that is punished, so when he awoke he was surprised to find the doors of the prison open.

Supposing: he was certain that at least some of them had escaped and that he would therefore be exposed to tortures ending in his being killed, so he decided to kill himself, because he would be sentenced to death in their place, as the Roman law stipulates.

entries.section: (5) The opening of the prison and the faith of the jailer

paragraphs.text: Paul could not see him, but God revealed the matter to him, so he cried out with a loud voice from the inner prison so that the jailer would hear him, asking him to refrain from killing himself because this is a great evil, and reassured him that everyone was there and no one had escaped.

entries.section: (5) The opening of the prison and the faith of the jailer

paragraphs.text: Called for a light: the word “light” in the original Greek is plural, that is, the jailer asked his assistants to bring a number of torches to make sure that all the prisoners were present.

Fell down: the jailer felt that Paul and Silas, whom they had arrested because of teachings foreign to the Roman pagan worship, must be men of God because of the earthquake that had occurred and the opening of the doors and the loosing of the fetters that followed it, so he prostrated himself before them.
Trembling: because he was before a great God who shakes the place, and He is the God of Paul and Silas.

entries.section: (5) The opening of the prison and the faith of the jailer

paragraphs.text: Sirs: this shows the extent of his respect and submission to them, and his readiness to accept preaching from them.

That I may be saved: the jailer cared about the salvation of his soul, for the miracle of the earthquake led him to care about his spiritual life and not only to be reassured that he would not be punished because the prisoners had not escaped.
Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ: because the foundation of salvation is the redemption of Christ.

They spake unto him: they explained to him the details of life with God within the Church, which includes the Holy Sacraments, the first of which is the sacrament of Baptism, which they performed for him (v. 33), and the means of grace such as prayer and fasting. All that were in his house: his wife, his children, his relatives and his servants.

The jailer brought Paul and Silas out of the prison and took them to his house, asking them to guide him to the way of salvation, for it seems that he had heard part of their preaching before and was moved by them, so they guided him to faith, he and the members of his household.

entries.section: (5) The opening of the prison and the faith of the jailer

paragraphs.text: The same hour of the night: it specifies here that the jailer brought them out during the night to his house and did not wait until the morning, and there he washed them of their wounds and they preached to him and then baptized him and the members of his household. Washed their stripes: from the wounds that had arisen on their backs from the beating, which had stuck to the filth of the inner prison, so they needed to be washed of them to relieve their pains.
All his: this must include the old and the young, and this confirms the importance of baptizing children so that they may receive salvation.

The jailer washed their wounds, since the miracle of the opening of the prison did not include the healing of their wounds, and he was baptized with all the members of his household, old and young, and they must have confessed their sins before Baptism, so they all received forgiveness and the new nature in the sacrament of Baptism.

entries.section: (5) The opening of the prison and the faith of the jailer

paragraphs.text: When he had brought them into his house: a confirmation of what he said in (v. 30), that the jailer brought them out of the prison to his house, that is, he wants to announce new events that took place in the house, namely the feast. The jailer set food before them in his house, since they had not eaten since the morning of the previous day when the evil spirit was cast out of the damsel. And of course the Apostle Paul performed for those gathered the sacrament of the Eucharist and gave them the Holy Mysteries, and the jailer was in joy, he and his household, after they believed.

God is searching for you however occupied you are with other things. Understand what happens around you, for it is messages from God to you to repent and believe in Him and return to Him, and make use of every opportunity to learn and know the way of life with God.

The magistrates were afraid because of the earthquake, lest this be the anger of the gods whom Paul and Silas proclaim, so they changed their opinion in the morning and instead of sentencing them to death they ordered their release.

After Paul and Silas had eaten with the jailer and the members of his household, they returned to the prison so as not to cause the jailer any problems, then the order of the magistrates arrived to release the two Apostles, and the jailer rejoiced because he had been in a predicament between his love for them and his duty as a jailer to guard them, and he informed the two Apostles of this happy news so that they might rejoice in it, since they received their freedom by it.
The magistrates fell into three errors in what they did to Paul and Silas, who were Romans, namely:
1- they beat them before the crowds, and this is a clear insult.
2- they ordered them to be bound.
3- they ordered them to be put in prison.

These things are not permitted by Roman law to be done to Romans, and therefore the magistrates are liable to trial, so Paul declared their citizenship and the errors into which the magistrates had fallen, and therefore refused to go out of the prison, as proof of the charge against the magistrates, and asked that the magistrates come themselves to the prison, that perhaps he might accept their apology and forgive them. He did this not out of pride but to give security and encouragement to the believers in Philippi, such as the jailer and Lydia, before the magistrates and all the people of the city.

The officers told the magistrates that the two Apostles were Romans, and they were afraid of what they had done to them, since they had become liable to trial and punishment that might reach execution and confiscation of property.

The magistrates came apologizing to the two Apostles and begging them to forgive them, and they brought them out of the prison and asked their leave that they depart from the city to prevent disturbance in it.

After the two Apostles left the prison, they went to the house of Lydia, where the believers usually met, and they told them of God’s work with them in the prison and also the news of the faith of the jailer and those in his house, and they were all comforted and encouraged.

Thus the Church of Philippi was founded, which later showed its strong love for Paul and its material offerings to help him in the ministry. It seems that Luke stayed in Philippi and did not complete the journey with Paul, as shown by the fact that he afterward spoke in the third person and not the first person until Paul returned to Philippi and took Luke with him (ch. 20:6).

Use your abilities and your position for the glory of God and not for your personal comfort, even if you bear many hardships for His sake, and work for the steadfastness of the Church and the ministry and the exalting of the name of Christ, for it is your first aim.
From Thessalonica to Athens

Paul and Silas left Philippi and journeyed on foot for a day, and reached the city of Amphipolis. They did not stay there either, because there was no Jewish synagogue there, for Paul used to take the Jews as the starting point of his preaching and evangelizing. Then they travelled for a third day and reached Thessalonica, the capital of Macedonia in the north of Greece, a well-known port.
The Scriptures: the books of the Old Testament.

Paul and Silas entered the synagogue, as was their custom, to preach first to the Jews. Although Paul was the apostle of the Gentiles, he cared for the Jews, besides using them as an entrance for evangelizing the Gentiles, some of whom attended the Jewish synagogue. They continued preaching for three Sabbaths in the synagogue, but they remained in the city for a longer time than this, during which St. Paul worked at the trade of tent-making (2 Thess 3:8), and there financial help reached them from Philippi twice.

St. Paul proved from the prophecies the necessity of the suffering of the expected Messiah, then His resurrection and His kingship, and this is what happened with Jesus; therefore Jesus is the Christ. For the Jews thought that the Messiah would be a king who would free them from the Romans, so they rejected the idea of His suffering and death, as the prophecies had said.

Consorted with: they joined in the faith of Paul and Silas, that is, they became members of the Church of Thessalonica. Some of the Jews believed, and many of the devout Greeks, who used to pray in the synagogue without becoming proselytes to Judaism, and also some of the women married to men of high position.

The lewd fellows of the baser sort (the market people): idle men who sit in the marketplace, Gentiles of the lowest classes. The Jews exploited them to stir up the Gentiles of the city, because they were Gentiles like them.
Set the city on an uproar: they stirred up the city with doubts against the teaching of Paul and Silas.
Jason: a Jew who believed the preaching of Paul and was his kinsman according to the flesh, and he hosted Paul and Silas in his house.

The Jews felt that faith in God and His blessings belonged to them alone, so they were greatly troubled when the Gentiles believed in God as they did. They hired wicked men to stir up the city and make it doubt Paul's preaching, and they attacked the house of Jason, Paul's kinsman, searching for the two Apostles.
The rulers of the city: Thessalonica was a free city, which Caesar allowed to be governed by men from among its own people, who had the authority to punish and to put to death.
Troubled: stirred up and disturbed with strange teachings.

They did not find Paul and Silas in the house of Jason, so they seized him and some of the Christians and took them to the rulers, and accused Paul and Silas of spreading strange teachings everywhere, and said that they had come to Thessalonica and begun to spread their teachings.

As usual, they mixed the religious accusation with a political one, claiming that Paul and Silas had taught against Caesar and proclaimed that Jesus is a king, and that Jason had hosted them in his house.
The people and the rulers were disturbed by this, and feared Caesar's revenge upon the city.

The rulers took a sum of money from Jason as a guarantee that he would send Paul and Silas out of the city, then released him and the Christians who had been seized. This shows the justice of these rulers and that they did not rush along behind the wicked Jews.

Do not stir up others against those who oppose you, and be careful in your speech lest you ascribe to them faults that are not in them. Rather, respect the opinion of others even if it differs from yours, and let God do what He wills even if it is against your opinion, for your agitation and anger will change nothing in the ordering of God's will, but will only increase your sins and your tension. Care only for your inner peace and for peace in your relationships with others.
Immediately: on the evening of the same day as the trial, so that things in the city might calm down, the rulers be reassured, and the uproar of the Jews subside.
Berea: it lies southwest of Thessalonica in the province of Macedonia, and the number of Jews in it is smaller than in Thessalonica.
The Christians sent Paul and Silas to Berea by night so that the Jews would not see them and harm them, and there the two Apostles began preaching in the synagogue of the Jews.
More noble: loftier in mind, understanding and breadth of heart.
With all readiness of mind: eagerness to understand what they had heard and to apply it in their lives.
Whether those things were so: making sure of the truth of the faith they had heard, with proofs from the prophecies found in the books of the Old Testament, so as to confirm this faith.
The Jews of Berea were better than the Jews of Thessalonica in their care to examine the prophecies and the Holy Scriptures, as the Lord said, "Search the scriptures" (Jn 5:39).
Many of the Jewish men believed, and of the Greek women who had joined the Jews, women of high rank, and also many of the Greek men.
The Jews of Thessalonica were enraged when they learned that the faith had spread in Berea, so they sent men from among them to stir up the people of Berea against Paul and Silas.

The Christians hastened to send Paul away as though he would travel by sea, in order to calm the anger of the Jews, but he travelled by land to Athens, the capital of Greece, although the land route is much longer. Silas and Timothy remained in Berea to complete the ministry, since the eyes of the wicked Jews were fixed on Paul and not on his companions.

Thus Paul ended his ministry in Macedonia, which was concentrated in three important places, Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea, as the divine vision had called him to serve in Macedonia (ch. 16:9); and afterward the Spirit of God directed him to serve in Athens, the center of Greek philosophy.

A group of the Christians of Berea accompanied Paul, and after arranging a place of residence for him in Athens, they returned to Berea and informed Silas and Timothy that Paul was waiting for them in Athens, so they travelled to him quickly.

Let your goal, which is the love of Christ and being with Him in eternity, always be before your eyes, and if obstacles confront you, flee from them and continue looking toward your goal. Do not be disturbed by opposition, for the devil is weak; he stirs up troubles, but he cannot stop your love and your striving toward God.

Paul was in Athens waiting for the arrival of Silas and Timothy, but he was troubled by the abundance of licentiousness in the pagan worship that was so widespread in the city, so that the historian Petronius said: it is easier to find a god in Athens than to find a man in it.
Paul preached only to the Jews in the synagogue and in the marketplace, because it was not only a place for buying and selling; many people gathered in it for dialogue and discussion.

Epicureans: followers of Epicurus, the Roman philosopher who appeared in the third century B.C., who neglected the idea of divinity, proclaimed that there is no reward or punishment, and permitted indulgence in desires. Stoics: followers of Zeno, the Greek philosopher who appeared in the third century before Christ, who proclaimed the importance of reason and considered God to be the world. He used to deliver his teachings in a portico, and his followers were called Stoics and were distinguished by pride.

St. Paul met a group of Greek philosophers belonging to the Epicureans and the Stoics, who thought that he was proclaiming strange gods because he was proclaiming Jesus and the resurrection from the dead. They supposed that he was proclaiming two gods, Jesus and the Resurrection, so they despised him and described him as a babbler, that is, one who does not understand what he says.
Areopagus: the highest philosophical council in Athens, in which they met to examine the various philosophies, ancient and modern.

These philosophers asked Paul to come with them to the council of the Areopagus, which met in a tiered place on the hill, to hear his new teaching, the like of which they had not heard before, so that they might examine this philosophy and decide whether it was right or wrong, and accordingly permit him to continue this teaching or stop it.
The most important thing to the people of Athens and its visitors was continual philosophical discussion, especially of new philosophies and ideas such as this new teaching that Paul was teaching.

Would that we spent our time on what is useful and not on vain talk. Avoid discussions that are of no benefit or that cause you to fall into mistaken ideas, and present Christ in your words and deeds in the form of love for those around you.

Paul began his sermon in the greatest philosophical council in Athens, which was famous throughout the whole world for its advancement in knowledge and philosophy at that time. He began by saying that he saw the great religiousness of the people of Athens, evident from the multitude of their idols. In this he commends a virtue in them, namely the religious inclination, even if it was in a mistaken direction, for it was a clear interest in religion, and this was in order to win their hearts to listen to him.

While Paul was passing through the streets of the city and getting to know its gods, he saw among their objects of worship one they called an unknown god. For a plague had spread in the city, and one of the philosophers advised them to release sheep throughout the city, and wherever a sheep lay down at the altar of any god, they were to offer it to that god to appease him. When some of the sheep lay down in places where there were no altars, they built altars and called them to an unknown god. Paul told them that he had come to preach to them the God whom they fear, for dread of His wrath, without knowing Him. By this he escaped the charge of preaching a new religion.

Paul said that this God is the one God, the Creator of the whole world, and that He is too great to dwell in temples built with hands, as St. Stephen had said in his speech before his martyrdom (ch. 7:48-50). This teaching is not against the presence of God in the tabernacle of meeting or the temple of Solomon in the Old Testament, or His presence in the Church of the New Testament, for He dwells there with His blessing, but His presence is not confined to them; rather He dwells in heaven and fills every place. In this Paul proclaims the oneness of God, and this is against the beliefs of the pagans in Athens.

Paul proclaimed that God has no need of the service and gifts of men, because He is the giver of life and of all blessings; but the offering of worship to God, in the Old or the New Testament, is a declaration of man's repentance, love and thanksgiving to Him.

Paul also proclaimed that God is the Creator of all from one origin, so there is no distinction between one race and another, but all are brothers, whom God distributed over the earth to inhabit it, each in the place and time suited to him, and He determined when a nation rises and when another falls. In this he rejects the arrogance of the Greeks toward the rest of mankind.
St. Paul asked them to seek God and establish a relationship with Him, for He is very near to them, not only with them but dwelling within them.

Paul made clear that God is the source of the life of all mankind, and he confirmed his words with sayings of the Greek poets, such as the Greek poet Aratus in 277 B.C. and the poet Cleanthes in 300 B.C., that we are His offspring. This shows St. Paul's study of Greek culture in Tarsus, in addition to his religious study at the feet of Gamaliel, the great teacher of the Jews. By this he proclaimed that God is very near to man, and not, as the Greeks think, that the gods dwell in distant places and are separate from mankind, or that matter came into being by itself.

The Apostle concluded from the sayings of the Greek poets that we are like God, as His offspring, so we know that the Godhead is not material but spiritual, like our spirits, which are in His likeness. If the essence of man is distinct from lifeless matter, then all the more the essence of God (the Godhead) is far higher than lifeless matter, that is, the idols. It is to be noticed that Paul did not rely in his proofs on verses of the Holy Scriptures, but on the sayings of pagan poets and philosophers, to persuade them to believe in God.
Now: since the preaching of the Gospel has begun in the whole world, as our Lord Jesus Christ commanded. All men: Jews and Gentiles.
Ignorance: he did not speak of evil and disobedience to God, but pleads an excuse for them, that they were idolaters through ignorance, and this is a gentle way of drawing the hearers to faith.
God calls all men to repentance, and promises them the forgiveness of their sins.
The world: all mankind, Jews and Gentiles.
In righteousness: without partiality or discrimination of race or person.
Whereof He hath given assurance unto all men: Christ accomplished redemption on the Cross, and offers salvation through preaching about Him, that men may believe and be saved.
Paul proclaimed the necessity of repentance, because God has appointed a day of judgment, on which He will send a man to judge all mankind, and he is Christ, whom He raised from the dead.
Some mocked: they were the Epicureans, who were immersed in desires and did not believe in the day of judgment, so they mocked Paul's teachings.

Others said, We will hear thee again of this matter: the others were the Stoics, who were more dignified and more receptive to faith in God. These asked to hear more details from him about this teaching, but they went back and rejected his teachings when they examined them, because they found them against their beliefs.

Despite the multiplicity of the religions of Athens, they all agreed that there is no resurrection after death, so when they heard the mention of the resurrection they mocked Paul, especially the Epicureans among them, and asked to postpone the rest of the talk to another time.
Departed: the council passed no judgment on him, but the majority of them rejected his teachings, as shown by his leaving free.

Dionysius: a Greek philosopher who was studying philosophy in Egypt at the time of the crucifixion of Christ, and saw the darkness that occurred at the sixth hour, that is, at noon, and said, as a student of astronomy, that this means that the God of the world is suffering. Then he returned to Greece and joined their philosophical council, the Areopagus, and when he heard Paul's teachings he believed in Christ. He has a homily (address) that is sometimes read on Great Friday. Paul departed from among them, and those who believed clave to him, among them a member of the philosophical council of the Areopagus, which required its members to be former judges over sixty years of age, whose name was Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.
Paul presented his message although many rejected it, but few accepted the faith.
Offer your love to all who are around you, even if many reject it, for some may accept it, and the rest may be affected after a while.
The ministry in Corinth and the end of the second journey

entries.section: (1) In Corinth and the faith of the ruler of the synagogue

paragraphs.text: Paul left Athens because he did not expect success in preaching there, and came to Corinth in the province of Hellas at the far south of Greece. It had a port on the east and another on the west, because it was the largest city in the south of Greece, which was called Achaia, just as Thessalonica was the largest city in the north, which was called Macedonia. In Corinth there was a temple for the worship of Venus, with a thousand priestesses who practiced vice with the worshippers of the temple as part of the worship. This shows the extent of the moral decay of this city, yet Paul remained in it a year and a half (v. 11), and the preaching succeeded greatly in it, and from it he wrote his two epistles to the Thessalonians.

entries.section: (1) In Corinth and the faith of the ruler of the synagogue

paragraphs.text: In Corinth there was a Christian of Jewish origin named Aquila, and with him his wife Priscilla.

They were originally from Pontus in northeastern Turkey, and were among the Jews whom Claudius Caesar had expelled from Rome, for he commanded the expulsion of all the Jews of Rome and forbade any Jew to live there because of the many disturbances that the Jews stirred up. So Paul came to them.

entries.section: (1) In Corinth and the faith of the ruler of the synagogue

paragraphs.text: The Jews were accustomed to teach their children a trade, whatever their educational and cultural level. So although Saul of Tarsus had learned philosophy and the religious sciences, he had trained in the trade of tent-making. When he visited Corinth and found Aquila and his wife working at the same trade, that encouraged him to stay with them and share this work with them, so as not to depend on anyone for the expenses of his living.

entries.section: (1) In Corinth and the faith of the ruler of the synagogue

paragraphs.text: St. Paul used to go every Sabbath to preach, discuss and persuade the Jews and the Greek proselytes in the synagogue concerning Christianity; on the other days he worked at tent-making, and he spent Sunday in spiritual worship with the Christians Aquila and Priscilla who were in Corinth.

entries.section: (1) In Corinth and the faith of the ruler of the synagogue

paragraphs.text: Pressed in spirit: with zeal and great fervor.
When Silas and Timothy, who had been in Macedonia in the north of Greece in the city of Thessalonica, came to Paul, he was preaching in Corinth to show the Jews that Jesus is the Christ, the Savior.

entries.section: (1) In Corinth and the faith of the ruler of the synagogue

paragraphs.text: The Jews opposed Paul with harsh words against Christ, so he shook his garments, as a sign of God's abandoning of the obstinate, and held them responsible for their rejection, declaring that he was innocent of their blood and that he would begin to preach to the Gentiles.

entries.section: (1) In Corinth and the faith of the ruler of the synagogue

paragraphs.text: Paul moved to the house of a man named Justus, next to the synagogue. He was one of the Greeks who worship God without becoming proselytes, and he had accepted faith in Christ. Paul took his house as a place from which to teach those who believed or were coming to the faith, because this house was suitable for that, being next to the synagogue, so everyone knew it and it was easy for them to meet with him.

entries.section: (1) In Corinth and the faith of the ruler of the synagogue

paragraphs.text: Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, had believed, he and his household, and St. Paul baptized him (1 Cor 1:14). This helped many Jews to enter the faith, and also the Greeks who were interested in the worship of God, for they came to hear Paul's teachings, and believed and were baptized. Thus the ministry succeeded greatly in a very wicked city, and this is proof of the work of God, who never lets us despair of doing good.

entries.section: (1) In Corinth and the faith of the ruler of the synagogue

paragraphs.text: I am with thee: since he feels that God is with him, he is reassured and encouraged to preach with zeal and to endure the opposition of the wicked, assured by God's promise that they cannot harm him or stop his preaching. I have much people: many souls will believe in Christ.

The Lord appeared to Paul in a vision to encourage him not to fear the violence of the opposition of the Jews of Corinth or the disdain of the Greeks there who were occupied with their desires, and to encourage him to continue preaching, declaring that He would keep him from all evil, because many would believe.

entries.section: (1) In Corinth and the faith of the ruler of the synagogue

paragraphs.text: Paul continued preaching Christianity for a year and a half, and founded a church there and organized its worship and responsibilities. He cared about this city because it is a port where many people coming from Rome, Alexandria and Ephesus meet, besides being an important city in the province of Achaia, that is, southern Greece.

When the wicked oppose you, do not despair and give up, for God supports you and He is stronger than all, knowing that some people do not accept the truth except after a long time, yet they may become stronger than the rest in their life with God.
Achaia: the Romans divided Greece into a northern province which they called Macedonia, and a southern one which they called Achaia, whose capital is Corinth, where the seat of the governorship was.
The judgment seat: it was customary for governors to sit on a seat of their own in a large square in the city to examine the cases and problems of the people.

The law: by it they mean the law of the Jews recognized by the Romans, and consequently preaching another religion under the name of Judaism was against Roman laws. It is possible that by the law they meant the Roman laws.

Gallio became proconsul of Achaia, who was the brother of the famous Roman philosopher Seneca, and he was a just man. At that time the Jews rose up with great violence against Paul and brought him to the governor's palace to be tried on a grave charge, namely that he was preaching a new religion not recognized by the Roman state, as Judaism was recognized by the Romans, a charge that led to expulsion or death.
Wrong: that is, depriving others of their rights and assaulting them.
Wicked lewdness: an evil intent that has evidence and leads to injustice.

Gallio did not wait for Paul to defend himself, but thought, as the Romans thought, that Christianity was a sect of Judaism, and that the problems of Christianity with the Jews were internal religious problems in which the Romans do not judge, but the Jews themselves. So Gallio declared to the Jews that this dispute was not within his competence, because it was a dispute about words and Jewish names, for Paul calls Jesus the Christ and they do not accept that, and he told them to judge him in their synagogue in a religious manner, where the greatest penalty would be to be cut off from the synagogue. But Gallio did not know that he had lost the opportunity of saving his own soul when he did not understand Paul's preaching, while the Lord delivered Paul from the Jewish plot.
Gallio drove the Jews away and rejected their case, especially since they were hated by the Greeks and the Romans because of their many troubles.

Gallio cared for none of those things: he allowed the pagans to beat Sosthenes to vent their anger, although this was contrary to the laws, but of course it was within certain limits. This shows his neglect of Jewish religious cases, for they were not his work as governor.

The Greeks of the people of Corinth seized the opportunity of the anger of Gallio the governor against the Jews, and beat Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue of the Jews, to humiliate them. The Jews had appointed Sosthenes ruler of their synagogue in succession to Crispus, who had believed in Christianity. But after this we read in (1 Cor 1:1) that Sosthenes also believed and accompanied St. Paul in his preaching.

Do not fear the plots of the wicked, for God is able to deliver you from them as He delivered Paul, however difficult the circumstances may appear, or however continuous the accusations and unceasing the insults, for in the end God turns all this to your good and keeps your inner peace, and even rewards you in eternity for what you endured.

entries.section: (3) The end of the second journey

paragraphs.text: Tarried there yet: after the agitation of the Jews against him calmed down, he continued for a time preaching in Corinth.
The brethren: the believers in Corinth.

Paul completed his preaching in Corinth for some time after that, then bade them farewell, returning to Syria. He had a vow upon him for a personal reason, according to the custom of the Law, for the Christians of Jewish origin such as Paul used to keep the commandments of the Law which they had been accustomed to throughout their lives before the faith, except the rites that were a type of Christ, such as the sacrifices.

After the period of the vow ended, Paul shaved his head, as is the custom of Nazirites, and this was in Cenchrea (the port of Corinth on its eastern side) (Num 6:1-21). Paul fulfilled the Mosaic law so as not to cause the Jews to stumble, although he did not require the Gentiles to keep it, because it is not necessary for obtaining salvation. Paul took Priscilla and Aquila with him. Here we see that the name of the wife is put before that of her husband, which shows the strength of her faith and her ministry.

entries.section: (3) The end of the second journey

paragraphs.text: Ephesus: the capital of Asia Minor (Turkey), an important port about three days from Corinth.
Left them there: he left Aquila and Priscilla to complete the preaching and ministry in Ephesus.
Entered into the synagogue: he was not troubled by the opposition of the Jews to him in Corinth, but continued to love them and began to preach to them in Ephesus that they might believe in Christ.
They all arrived at Ephesus in Turkey, and Paul left Aquila and his wife there, and entered the synagogue to preach and discuss with the Jews as was his custom.

entries.section: (3) The end of the second journey

paragraphs.text: The Jews in Ephesus responded to Paul's sermons and asked him to stay with them and complete his preaching among them, but he did not agree; rather he travelled, because he wanted to attend the coming feast of Pentecost in Jerusalem to complete the procedures of his vow and burn the hair he had shaved in the temple, and so that he could preach to the Jews gathered in Jerusalem at the feast of Pentecost, who had come to it from all parts of the world. He promised the people of Ephesus to return to them on his coming (third) journey, and indeed he returned and stayed with them three years (ch. 20:31).

entries.section: (3) The end of the second journey

paragraphs.text: Caesarea: it is considered the port of Jerusalem, that is, the nearest port to it.

Paul arrived by sea from Ephesus at Caesarea in Palestine, then from there to Jerusalem to greet the Church and the Apostles and tell them what had happened on his second journey. This was his fourth visit to Jerusalem. Then he returned to Antioch for the last time, to rest a little before beginning his third journey, on which he set out from Antioch, and he did not return to it for the rest of his life on earth.
His second journey lasted three years (from A.D. 51 to 54).
What great striving Paul accomplished!... May your life be as fruitful for the Lord.
Do you use all your time in useful things? May your goal, which is the love of Christ, always be before your eyes, that it may give you zeal for spiritual work.

entries.section: (4) The beginning of the third journey from Antioch

paragraphs.text: Galatia and Phrygia: two regions in Asia Minor, which is Turkey.

Paul stayed in Antioch for less than a year, then began his third missionary journey, as usual in Turkey and then Europe. The journey took the period from A.D. 54 to 58, and is recorded from (ch. 18:23) to (ch. 21:17). The route of the journey was as follows:

From Antioch (Syria) by land to Tarsus (Turkey), then by land to Derbe (Turkey), and after that by land to Iconium (Turkey) and from there by land to Antioch (Turkey). From there he went by sea to Ephesus (Turkey), where the riot of Demetrius and the craftsmen took place. From there he went by sea to Mitylene (Turkey), then by sea to Troas (Turkey), and after that by sea to Philippi (Greece). Then by land to Thessalonica (Greece), and from there he went by sea to Corinth in the province of Hellas (southern Greece), and from there by land to Berea (Greece), and from there he went by sea to Philippi (Greece), then by sea to Troas (Turkey), where the Apostle Paul raised the young man Eutychus from death. After that he went by land to Assos (Turkey), and from there by sea to Mitylene (Turkey), and after it by sea to Samos (Turkey), then by sea to Miletus (Turkey), and from there he sailed by sea to Cos (Turkey), and afterward went by sea to Rhodes (Greece), and after it by sea to Tyre (Palestine), and from there he went by land to Caesarea (Palestine), and finally arrived by land at Jerusalem.

entries.section: (4) The beginning of the third journey from Antioch

paragraphs.text: Before Paul reached Ephesus, where he had earlier left Aquila and Priscilla, a Christian of Jewish origin named Apollos came to it. He was one of the Jews of Alexandria, gifted in discussion and a student of the Old Testament.

entries.section: (4) The beginning of the third journey from Antioch

paragraphs.text: Mighty: deeply versed and living the spiritual meanings.
The way of the Lord: Christianity.
Fervent in spirit: full of zeal and spiritual power.
The baptism of John: the teachings of John, his baptizing of the people, and his witness to Christ.

Apollos was a spiritual man, who lived what he said and felt, but he knew nothing of Christianity except the witness of John the Baptist about Christ, and likewise he knew nothing of His teachings, His death and His resurrection.

entries.section: (4) The beginning of the third journey from Antioch

paragraphs.text: It seems that Aquila and Priscilla were accustomed to attend the synagogue, so they heard Apollos preaching in it and discovered his knowledge of the death and resurrection of Christ, so they took him to them and expounded to him the rest of Christianity accurately. They spoke to him of the Cross, the Resurrection, redemption, the descent of the Holy Spirit and the Sacraments, and he listened humbly although he was a great orator and philosopher, and believed everything.

entries.section: (4) The beginning of the third journey from Antioch

paragraphs.text: Apollos went to Corinth, the capital of Achaia in the south of Greece, to preach in it, and the Christians of Ephesus gave him a letter of recommendation to the believers in Corinth so that they would receive him without apprehension, and this was customary among the churches. So he strengthened the faith of the believers and answered the opposing Jews, and this helped in the steadfastness of the Church there.

entries.section: (4) The beginning of the third journey from Antioch

paragraphs.text: Apollos proved to the Jews of Corinth that Jesus is the Christ from the prophecies and books of the Old Testament, and answered their opposition and silenced them, because he was filled with the Holy Spirit and had studied the science of rhetoric and persuasion in the school of Alexandria.

Every person has a gift that he ought to use for the service of Christ, like Apollos. So try to discover your gifts by prayer and the guidance of your father of confession, and use them for the benefit of the Church; you are responsible for investing them and you will be called to account for that, and at the same time you will enjoy the blessings of this gift for the growth of your life together with the others who benefit from it.
Paul's ministry in Ephesus

entries.section: (1) Paul's ministry in Ephesus and his miracles

paragraphs.text: Ephesus: the capital of Asia Minor (Turkey), located on its western coast. It had the temple of Artemis, which is counted among the seven wonders of the world. Paul was concerned to make it a center for serving the churches of Turkey, just as he made Corinth a center for serving the churches of Greece.

At the beginning of the third journey, Paul was on a journey by land through Turkey, and he reached Ephesus while Apollos was preaching in Corinth, and found Christians who were disciples of John the Baptist, who knew nothing of Christ except John's witness to Him.

entries.section: (1) Paul's ministry in Ephesus and his miracles

paragraphs.text: Paul learned from them that they had believed in Christ through Apollos, who knew nothing of Christ except the witness of John the Baptist to Him, and consequently they did not know the Holy Spirit and had not received Christian Baptism.

entries.section: (1) Paul's ministry in Ephesus and his miracles

paragraphs.text: Paul completed their evangelizing, explaining that the baptism of John is a baptism of repentance, and is a preparation for Christian Baptism by the Holy Spirit, through which we receive the salvation that Christ accomplished on the Cross.

entries.section: (1) Paul's ministry in Ephesus and his miracles

paragraphs.text: When the people of Ephesus heard, they believed and were baptized in the name of Christ, and so received the blessing of the sacrament.

entries.section: (1) Paul's ministry in Ephesus and his miracles

paragraphs.text: Paul laid his hands on them, by his priestly authority as a bishop, and the Holy Spirit came upon them, that is, the sacrament of the Holy Myron, and they spoke with tongues and languages. They were about twelve men, not counting the women and children. These were a group of the people of Ephesus; as for the others, they had complete faith in Christ and had received Baptism and the Holy Myron, and they were those who believed through Paul on the previous visit.

entries.section: (1) Paul's ministry in Ephesus and his miracles

paragraphs.text: The kingdom of God: faith in Christ who reigns over hearts, and that we have the eternal Kingdom. Paul began, as was his custom, preaching to the Jews in the synagogue, and continued in it for three months.

entries.section: (1) Paul's ministry in Ephesus and his miracles

paragraphs.text: Hardened: they rejected the Christian faith and opposed it.
That way: Christianity.
Disputing: preaching, persuading, and showing the error or customs of Judaism.

The Jews began to blaspheme and revile Christianity, so Paul left the synagogue and took the Christians with him, using one of the schools as a place for preaching; it belonged to a Greek philosopher named Tyrannus, who had believed.
Thus those who had asked him to stay with them on his previous journey turned against him (ch. 18:20).

entries.section: (1) Paul's ministry in Ephesus and his miracles

paragraphs.text: Paul continued preaching in the school for two years until the message spread among the Jews and the Greeks in western Turkey, in the city of Ephesus and around it, in the seven churches to which the Apostle John wrote.

entries.section: (1) Paul's ministry in Ephesus and his miracles

paragraphs.text: Aprons: these are work-aprons worn while working at tent-making.

God wrought special miracles by the hand of the Apostle Paul, for they used to touch his body with handkerchiefs and aprons and then send them to the sick, and they were healed, and the evil spirits went out of those who had them. This shows us the importance of the blessing of the saints, their relics, their intercession and their monasteries, which we must be careful to obtain.

In proportion as the wicked oppose you, the grace of God will support you in a way you cannot imagine. So continue to offer your love and your service, and flee from confronting evil, for your aim is to do good. Do not argue with one who does not want to hear, but persuade with love and long-suffering the one who is ready to respond.
Vagabond (itinerant): they travel from one country to another to practice their profession, which is the use of magic to cast out demons.
Exorcists: exorcism is the recitation of certain words and phrases to cast out demons.
Call over: they repeat a name.
We adjure you: we command you to obey.

Jesus whom Paul preacheth: to distinguish Him from the many Jews whose name was Jesus. Some Jews claimed the ability to cast out demons by acts of magic which the Jewish law forbids. They used magic words, among them the name Jehovah, to cast out demons. When they heard of the power of the Apostle Paul to cast out demons in the name of Christ, they too tried to use the name of Jesus Christ in their magic incantations.

The itinerant Jews who claimed to cast out demons were sons of a Jewish chief priest named Sceva. He was the head of one of the twenty-four priestly divisions of the Jewish priests who served the temple, each division in its turn (Lk 1:8). Perhaps this Sceva had left Judaism for paganism.

A great miracle occurred, which is that the evil spirit answered the sons of Sceva, confessing the power of the name of Christ and the faith of Paul, and attacked the men and beat them and tore their clothes, so that they fled naked, that is, with torn clothes, and wounded.

The news spread among the people of Ephesus, and they learned the power of the name of Jesus Christ, and they feared Him and His disciple Paul, whose power was shown to be distinct from that of the magicians. So the name of Christ was magnified, which helped the spread of faith in Him.

The greatness of the name of Christ and the fear of it encouraged many of the new believers to confess their former faults, and this is a reference to the sacrament of open confession and its practice in the early Church.

Fifty thousand pieces of silver: if what is meant is fifty thousand shekels (the Jewish silver shekel being 11.5 grams), the amount would be approximately 600 kg of silver; but if what is meant is the Greek drachma (weighing 4 grams of silver), the amount would be about 200 kg. The total price of the books of magic was fifty thousand pieces of silver, and this is a large sum.

Many of the Christians who had practiced magic before their faith burned the books of magic, and in spite of the material loss they considered their gain by faith in Christ greater and more precious. This is practical repentance and practical faith, for they were not content with a profession of faith or words of repentance, but completed them by their deeds, since they got rid of the books of magic.
The word of God and His Church grew mightily. Here we notice two things:
First: the name of Christ is not a magic charm that casts out evil spirits, but we must have strong faith in this name and a spiritual life that bears witness to this faith.

Second: magic is forbidden in all its kinds, among them divination, that is, telling of unknown things, the interpretation of dreams, the declaring of secrets unknown to the public, the discovery of stolen goods, the discovery of treasures, the making of love charms between people or between a young man and a girl, the reading of fortunes and of days by observing luck in order to know the lucky days from the unlucky, the making of amulets, incantation with unintelligible words, and charms with magic phrases to drive away sickness and weakness. All of these are resorting to the work of Satan.

Do not be preoccupied with the future, for your God arranges the best for you. And do not fear anyone, for your protector is the God of gods. Do not seek knowledge apart from God lest you fall into the hand of Satan, and do not enter into these things even by way of joking, lest your heart be drawn to them and your mind be occupied with them.
And know that the devil waits for a moment of weakness in you in order to fight you.

And if you have sinned and transgressed God's commandments in any magical matters, hasten to confession and Holy Communion, burn everything you have, and be diligent in prayer and in reading the Holy Bible.

After about three years of preaching in Ephesus, the Apostle Paul resolved to go to the north of Greece, called Macedonia, and its south, called Achaia, and to collect gifts for the Church of Jerusalem, then to return with them to it, and then to travel to Rome to preach there. Thus he would have preached in Jerusalem, the center of Judaism in the world, and Athens, the center of philosophy, and Rome, the center of authority.
Paul sent Timothy and Erastus ahead of him to Macedonia, and he remained to complete the ministry in Ephesus.
That way: Christianity.
At that time a great riot occurred in Ephesus because of the spread of Christianity.
Silver shrines: small silver statues of the goddess Artemis, which they place in their houses and carry on their journeys to protect and bless them.

Demetrius the silversmith worked at making small silver idols, which were placed in symbolic shrines of the idols. He was the leader of a large group of silversmiths who worked at this and made great gains.

Demetrius gathered the craftsmen together with all those working in the trade of making statues of the goddess Artemis, and told them that their ample livelihood was in danger because of the success of Paul's ministry in Asia in general and in Ephesus in particular, and that if Paul's ministry continued their livelihood would stop and the greatness of Artemis would become worthless. He showed concern for Artemis in order to stir up the people, although his real aim was his own material gain, and that of those with him.

When religion was mixed with the craftsmen's livelihood, they became very angry and began to magnify Artemis with loud shouting, not only out of esteem and attachment to their gods, but even more out of fear for their gains.
The theater: a large arena with open tiers that held 30,000 spectators.

The whole city was thrown into confusion and the crowds rushed into the Roman amphitheater called "the theater," and seized two of Paul's companions, because, being pagans, they did not distinguish between Christianity and Judaism, and thought that Paul's preaching was one of the plots of the Jews, who were hated by them.
Paul tried to go to the theater to defend his two companions, but the believers prevented him, fearing for him because of the agitation of the people, owing to their attachment to Artemis.
The chief of Asia: ten of the great men of Asia, which is a part of Turkey, and its wealthy men, who are concerned with arranging the feasts of the gods and spending on them.

Some of the chief of Asia were friends of Paul, and had not necessarily believed, but were bound to him only by ties of affection. These were in Ephesus because of the celebrations there for Artemis, so they sent to Paul that he should hide and not expose himself to the dangers of the rioting people.

The shouting of the people in the arena was great, for they felt that there was an attack on their city and on their gods, but they did not know from whom this attack came or for what reason, so it was an agitation without any definite cause.

The pagans seized a Jew named Alexander, who was an orator, and the Jews had pushed him forward to make a defense for them, that is, to clear them of the charge of enmity to Artemis, so that Paul and those with him, that is, the Christians, would be the only ones condemned, because the pagans still considered Christianity a sect of the Jews. So Alexander beckoned to the crowd to be silent and give him an opportunity to speak to them.

When Alexander tried to speak and the crowds knew that he was a Jew, whether from his appearance or his speech or because some knew him, the shouting and agitation increased for about two hours, proclaiming their exaltation of their gods who were insulted by their enemies the Jews, for the pagans hated the Jews.
The townclerk: the one responsible for recording the records of the court, and this was a high position in the city.
Jupiter: the planet Jupiter, for they supposed that the statue of Artemis had come down from it, that is, had fallen from heaven to earth.
Rashly: that is, with rioting and agitation, so that you fall into errors for which you are punished.

The clerk quieted the shouters, for he was a wise man, and he affirmed to them the greatness of their gods, which is beyond doubt, and whose wooden statue they supposed had come down from the planet Jupiter, the symbol of the god of gods; and if the greatness of Artemis is evident, why their agitation?

The clerk pointed out that they had fallen into an error, which was the seizing of Aristarchus and Gaius without any charge brought against them, for they had not been caught in robbing the temple of Artemis or attacking her worship. Paul was not reviling Artemis personally, but was exalting Christ before men by his preaching.
Implead one another: each one declares his argument and his evidence.
Deputies: judges and advocates.

The clerk declared the error of this disturbance and that the proper way is to bring a case before the court, and he also fixed the problem on Demetrius and those with him. If they had a complaint or accusation, there was no need to stir up the whole city, but let them present it in court to be looked into, and let the complainant declare his accusation and the accused defend himself.

The clerk added that if Demetrius or anyone else of those gathered in the theater had any other complaint, it should be brought in a lawful assembly, which is the court of appeal that meets every three months in the presence of the judges.

The clerk made clear that this agitation had no legal basis and exposed the city to Roman anger so that they would punish it, since their gathering was unlawful and would be considered a rebellion and a riot that provokes the anger of the authority in Rome.

Thus the clerk dismissed the crowd by his wise speech, for he praised their concern for worship and their guarding of the temple of Artemis, and they calmed down when he warned them of the error of their agitation without a lawful assembly and their exposure to punishment, so they were persuaded and dispersed.

Our God often uses unbelievers, such as the chief of Asia or the town clerk, in rescuing His children, for He is the Controller of all things for their good, so that we may not be anxious in troubles. So do not think beyond your strength in solving problems, and trust that your God, for whom you pray, is able to solve them in ways that do not occur to your mind. Remember, O Lord, Your servant R.N. The move to Greece, then the farewell to Ephesus on the way back

After the end of the riot in Ephesus, Paul bade farewell to the Church to go to Greece, crossing the Aegean Sea to begin by ministering in the north of Greece (Macedonia). Word had reached him of the existence of many problems in the Church of Corinth in the south of Greece, so he wrote his first and second epistles to the Corinthians.
Greece: the region in the south of the land of Greece, also called Achaia, in which Corinth is located.
After Paul finished his ministry in Macedonia, he came to Greece.

Paul stayed in Greece three months in the city of Corinth, then set out to return to Syria to end his third journey, but he learned that the Jews had devised a plot to kill him on the way back by sea from Cenchrea, the eastern port of Corinth, to Caesarea in Palestine, and therefore all decided that he should not return that way, but should go up by land from the south of Greece to its north, then by sea to Turkey, and from there by sea to Palestine, to avoid this plot.

A large group accompanied Paul for fear of the problems of the road, among them Sopater of Berea in Greece, who was one of Paul's kinsmen, and others from Turkey such as Gaius of Derbe, and Trophimus, who was from Ephesus. They helped him in preaching, and carried with him the gifts from the churches of the Gentiles to the poor of Jerusalem.
All these went ahead of Paul by sea to Troas in Turkey, so that he might reach them from Greece.
And Luke joined him, as shown by the fact that he begins speaking here in the first person, and he continued to accompany him until his first imprisonment in Rome in A.D. 62.

Paul and Luke and another group sailed by sea, after the seven days of unleavened bread that follow the Passover of the Jews, by way of Philippi, for five days to Troas in Turkey. In this Troas, five years earlier, a Macedonian man had appeared in a vision to Paul and called him to serve in Philippi in Europe. And here Paul returns once more to Troas in Turkey on his way back from the third journey, heading for Caesarea in Palestine, and he stayed in Troas seven days.

Flee from evil, for this is not weakness but true strength and wisdom. Your fleeing gives you a greater opportunity to continue positive work, and keeps your inner peace, and you also save the wicked from falling into the sin of wronging you.
The first day of the week: that is, Sunday (Jn 20:19). To break bread: that is, the celebration of the sacrament of the Eucharist.

The Lord's Day was Sunday, and it began from the evening of the Sabbath, when the believers gather around the sacrament of Holy Communion, and after it Paul began to preach and prolonged his preaching until midnight, since it was a farewell sermon, for he had arranged to travel on Sunday morning.

The lamps here declare that it was night, and the Church has been accustomed in every Liturgy, even if the light of day is clear, to light many lamps as a reference to Christ the Light of the world, whom we celebrate in the Liturgy. Many lights were lit in the upper room, which is on the third floor of the house in which they were gathered.
And the many lamps confirm that they gathered for prayer and preaching, and not for evil and unclean deeds as the enemies of Christianity accused them.

A young man named Eutychus was sitting in the window (the opening) because of the crowding in the upper room. Perhaps the many lamps with their heat, and the large number of those gathered, helped the young man to fall asleep, so he fell to the ground floor and died.

Paul went down from the upper room to the courtyard of the house, and did as Elijah and Elisha did (1 Kgs 17:21, 2 Kgs 4:33-35), for he lay upon the young man and embraced him and prayed until his spirit returned to him, and he tried to hide the greatness of the miracle by saying, "for his life is in him."

After he raised him from the dead, they completed the prayers and partook of the Holy Mysteries, and Paul continued his talk until dawn and then departed. This shows Paul's zeal for teaching, and the concern of the believers there for spiritual discipleship, since they stayed up all night.
All went out rejoicing and comforted by the great miracle, which was the raising of the young man from the dead.

Humility and hiding the miracles that the Lord works by the hand of the servant is a great virtue. So do not seek the praise of others, or ask them their opinion of your services so that they will magnify you, or tell them of your labors in the ministry so that they will praise you, for by this you lose the divine reward and fall into pride.

After Luke and Paul's companions spent a week in Troas, they boarded the ship from there to Assos, which is considered the port of the city of Troas and lies 24 miles south of it, while Paul came on foot so as to be alone for prayer and meditation on the way, as Christ used to do. The land route was half the distance of the sea route, that is, about seven hours' walk.
When Paul reached the port of Assos, he boarded the ship with his companions, and they all travelled to the city of Mitylene, about 30 miles from it.

After that, Paul and his companions travelled south to Chios, which is an island, and continued southward and went to Samos, which is also an island, about seventy miles from Chios, and from there he headed to Trogyllium, then from there went south to Miletus, which is 30 miles from Ephesus.
To sail by Ephesus: so he went to Miletus, which is 30 miles south of it. Asia: the region in which the city of Ephesus lies.

If it were possible for him: since the winds are not dependable, the ship might take longer in the voyage. The Apostle Paul did not want to pass through Ephesus lest he be late for the day of Pentecost in Jerusalem on his return journey, so he reached Miletus and sent for the priests of Ephesus and met them there, because the Church of Ephesus was urgently asking him to stay with them for a while. All this was so that he might attend the Jewish feast of Pentecost in Jerusalem, and complete the procedures of his personal vow and preach to the Jews gathered at the feast.

Paul cared for solitude and meditation, so he travelled alone from Troas to the port of Assos. It is good for a person to have times of quiet, prayer, praise and meditation away from the noise of the world and the concerns of company. Let there be for you every day, or at least every week, a quiet time with God in your house or any quiet place, to pray and meditate on the word of God, and open your heart with love toward Him and review your life, so that you are filled with His grace.

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: Paul wanted to meet the priests of Ephesus to give them his charge, so he sent for them to Miletus.

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: This sermon is one of the most important sermons of the Apostle Paul recorded in the Bible, and is fit to be a model for priests and servants by which they measure themselves, for he, as a teacher, guides his disciples out of his practical spiritual experience and shows them how the ministry becomes fruitful and successful. He pointed to his conduct among them from the time he began preaching in Ephesus three years before, serving with humility and prayers, with tears and many trials which he suffered from the Jews. This sermon can be divided into three parts:
1- His ministry among them and the reasons for his quick departure from them (vv. 18-24).
2- Faithfulness in the ministry and guarding against the dangers of the future (25-31).
3- Urging them to follow his conduct among them (vv. 32-35).

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: Paul pointed to three qualities in his ministry in the Church of Ephesus, which are:
1- Humility in all his dealings with them and his care for them.
2- His tenderness and compassion for sinners, which appears in tearful prayers before God.
3- His endurance of many sufferings from the opposing Jews.

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: Paul made clear his faithfulness in his ministry and in delivering all the spiritual truths to them, whether in his public preaching in the synagogue of the Jews or the school of Tyrannus, and also his individual ministry by visiting houses.

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: The subject of Paul's preaching in Ephesus, whether to the Jews or to the pagans, was two things:
1- Repentance and abandoning former sins.
2- Faith in Christ the Savior.

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: Paul told them that he was going to Jerusalem, led by the guidance of the Holy Spirit, not knowing the details of what would happen to him there. He is thus an example of reliance on God and submission to His will.

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: Bonds: chains or ropes with which one is bound.
The Holy Spirit declared to Paul that he would face afflictions and tribulations during his preaching in the various countries, without specifying their details.

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: Paul also declared his concern for his goal, which is the completion of his missionary ministry for Christ, sacrificing everything and even his life as well; indeed this self-giving in the ministry is the source of his joy, because it is for the sake of Christ.

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: Paul expected that he would not see the priests of Ephesus again in the body, so he gave them the summary of his commandments and his pastoral teachings.

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: The counsel of God: the teachings of the Church.

He declared to them that he is now not responsible before God if any of them perish through disobedience to the word of God, because he preached among them with all faithfulness and did not fall short.

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: Paul charged them to take heed, whether for the salvation of their own souls personally or the salvation of the souls of those they serve. For the price of the human soul is the blood of Christ our God.

We notice here that the early Church had priests and bishops, though the responsibilities and pastoral limits between the two ranks had not yet taken shape into the form in which they exist now. We also notice Paul's faith in the oneness of the divine and human nature of Christ at one and the same time, calling His blood "the blood of Christ." This verse proves the divinity of Christ, because God as spirit has no blood. This verse applies only to Christ, God incarnate, for He is God and man at one and the same time.

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: Paul declares to them that after him there will come innovators and heretics such as Nicolaus, whose heresy is mentioned in the Book of Revelation (2:6), and he likens them to wolves, which have no pity on the lambs but devour them.

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: Some heretics will arise from among the people of Ephesus themselves, who will try by false teachings to deceive many.

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: Therefore perseverance in the ministry is required, as Paul did, for he served among them whether the time was convenient for him or not, and he served day and night without rest and with everyone for a period of three years, proclaiming the truth and rebuking sinners and all people lest they fall into sin, but his teachings and firmness were mingled with compassion and tenderness and prayer with tears for all.

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: The time had come to leave them in the hand of Christ, to return the deposit, which is their souls, that God might shepherd them by His word in the Holy Bible, which is able to build them up until they reach their eternal inheritance with all the saints in heaven.

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: Paul made clear his integrity in the ministry, without covetousness for their material goods.

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: Paul worked at tent-making with his hands to support himself and the servants with him, although it is natural for the priest or the consecrated servant to take his material needs from those he serves, so that he may remain free for the ministry (Lk 10:7).

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: Thus he set an example for them to follow, so that they might help the poor from the labor of their hands, in fulfillment of the Lord's saying in praise of giving more than receiving, a saying that the four Gospels did not record, but which the believers handed down.

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

paragraphs.text: Paul knelt with them praying, and they were moved and weeping at parting from him, and they embraced him and kissed him.

entries.section: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus
