paragraphs.text: They then accompanied Paul to the ship to begin the return journey by sea to Palestine, and their hearts were grieved at parting from him and at being deprived of seeing him a second time.

When the servant reviews the details of his ministry and finds that what was accomplished by the grace of God was according to the divine purpose and will, he is comforted for his labors and awaits his eternal reward. So thank God for all that He has done with you and through you in the ministry, and take care to disciple others faithfully, declaring to them everything you have known from God and your teachers about the spiritual life.
The return to Jerusalem and the arrest of Paul

The return journey of Paul and his companions to Jerusalem began. After they left Miletus and bade farewell to the priests of Ephesus and the believers there, they headed to the island of Cos and from it to the island of Rhodes in the Mediterranean Sea, and reached the port of Patara in southern Turkey.
After that they boarded a ship heading for Phoenicia (present-day Lebanon).
As they crossed the sea, they saw Cyprus on their left from afar. And they sailed to Tyre, the most important port of Phoenicia, so that the ship might unload its cargo before continuing its voyage.
Through the Spirit: the Holy Spirit revealed to some of the prophets among the believers of Tyre that Paul would meet persecutions and dangers in Jerusalem.

During their stay in Tyre they visited the Christians there for seven days, the time for the ship to unload its cargo. The believers were telling Paul not to go to Jerusalem, because the Holy Spirit had informed them that he would meet troubles in it. This was not a divine declaration forbidding him to travel there, but only a disclosure of the persecutions he would meet.

At the end of the seven days, when the ship was ready to sail, all accompanied him on his way, and they knelt and prayed together on the shore. The hearts of all were attached to him, for the men, women and children came to bid him farewell after spending seven days with him.
After bidding Paul farewell, the people of Tyre returned to their homes, and he and his companions completed their journey.

If problems appear on the path of your spiritual life or your ministry, do not be disturbed or turn back from walking with God, as long as the Holy Spirit within you guides you to continue, confirmed by your father of confession and your guides. Christ will support you, and you will experience Him more deeply than you feel Him in ordinary times.
Then they came by sea from Tyre to Ptolemais, that is, Acre, and greeted the Christians who were there and stayed with them one day.
Caesarea: a port on the Mediterranean Sea, seventy miles from Jerusalem.
Paul's companions travelled with him by land to Caesarea of Palestine, and stayed in the house of Philip the deacon, who baptized the Ethiopian eunuch and was one of the seven deacons (6:5-6).
Philip had four unmarried daughters who had the gift of prophecy.
Paul stayed with Philip a long time so as not to go to Jerusalem except at the feast of Pentecost, until a Christian prophet from Judea named Agabus came (ch. 10:27-30).
Girdle: a belt.

Agabus took Paul's girdle and bound his own hands and feet, and said by a declaration of the Holy Spirit that the man who owns this girdle, that is, Paul, would be bound by the Jews at Jerusalem and delivered into the hands of the Gentiles, that is, the Roman authority.
When Paul's friends heard this, they besought him, together with the people of Acre, not to go up to Jerusalem.
Paul declared to those around him that their pity for him pained him, for it was contrary to his feelings, which were readiness to endure sufferings and even death for the sake of Christ.
Paul's friends ceased from asking, submitting to the ordering of God.

After completing their stay in Caesarea, they made ready and travelled by land to Jerusalem, and some of the believers from Caesarea came with them, and they stayed in Jerusalem in the house of a Christian man of Cypriot origin named Mnason.
Be discerning of the words of those who pity you; if they hinder your spiritual life, do not listen to them, and thank them for their love.
Paul entered Jerusalem for the fifth time, and the believers in it rejoiced at meeting him.

Paul met with James the brother of the Lord, that is, the cousin of the Lord Christ, and bishop of Jerusalem, and all the priests of Jerusalem attended the meeting. Thus the third missionary journey came to an end.

Paul explained to those present the details of the Lord's work with him in the ministry to the Gentiles, and how many churches were founded in Europe, and the alms he had collected for the needy in the Church of Jerusalem.
Myriads: ten thousand, and what is meant is a great number.
Those present rejoiced and glorified God, and informed Paul that there were many Christians of Jewish origin who held fast to the Jewish law even after becoming Christians.

The false brethren distorted Paul's reputation. These were the converts of Jewish origin who proclaimed the necessity of becoming Jews before believing in Christ. The Jews who did not believe hated Paul, and the Jews who believed doubted him, so they spread the report that Paul teaches that no law-observance should be carried out and forbids circumcision. By this they stirred everyone up against him.

It was expected that the Jews, both converts and non-converts, would come to Jerusalem during the days of the feast of Pentecost, and of course they would meet Paul, of whom they had heard that he is against their law, so the Church thought of a way to calm their feelings against him.
Purify thyself with them: take part in fulfilling the Jewish law.

That they may shave their heads: the law of the Nazirite was that he should not shave his head except at the end of the period of the vow. To disprove the accusations directed against Paul, the members of the Church advised him to take with him four converted men who had vows upon them, and to spend on them from his own money as the well-to-do among the Jews do for the poor, so that they might shave their heads and offer the sacrifices required at the end of the vow, so that all would see his keeping of the Law and know the falsehood of the rumors against him.

They reassured Paul that they had told the Christians of Gentile origin not to keep anything of the Jewish law except abstaining from what is sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from fornication. So what they asked of Paul was merely to calm the Jews who were in an uproar against him in Jerusalem, and it was not required of Christians in general throughout the world.

Paul obeyed and took the men and purified himself with them according to the Law, and notified the priests that one week remained to complete the period of the vow, so that they might prepare the required sacrifices.

When the remaining seven days of the period of the vow were about to end, which are the most important days of the vow, in which the worship and purifications are offered, the Jews who had come from the region of Ephesus in western Turkey stirred up the crowds against him and laid hands on him, crying out and calling for the help of the fanatical Jews, and claiming that Paul had brought pagan men into the temple to defile it and had not been careful to keep them in the court of the Gentiles. This is a charge that deserves death, because he had defiled the temple.

The Jews' accusation against Paul was not true, but was an inference of theirs, because they had seen with him in the city Trophimus the Ephesian, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.
All Jerusalem was moved, and the Jews hurried toward the temple and seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, then shut its doors, being careful that it should not be defiled.

The Jews beat Paul severely with the intent of killing him. Next to the temple was a fortress in which was a commander who led a cohort of 1,000 soldiers, named Claudius Lysias. When the news reached him from the Roman soldiers stationed next to the temple, he immediately took centurions with their soldiers, that is, no fewer than 300 soldiers, and ran down upon them, rushing through the crowds to put an end to the riot, and commanded them not to beat Paul.

How necessary it is for a person to be careful in his conclusions, lest he wrong others by supposing that what he has imagined is true. And how anger cancels the minds of men and makes their actions irrational and mad. So do not rush in your words and actions, and rely on prayer so that you do not wrong others when they are not at fault, and do not agree with those around you without thinking, for they may be mistaken.

entries.section: (4) Paul in the custody of the Roman government

paragraphs.text: The commander came near to Paul and took him and bound him with two chains to two soldiers to guard him, and asked who he was and what he had done.

entries.section: (4) Paul in the custody of the Roman government

paragraphs.text: The commander could not understand anything because of the intensity of the uproar, so he commanded that Paul be taken into the fortress.

entries.section: (4) Paul in the custody of the Roman government

paragraphs.text: Away with him: take him away to be killed, that is, kill him without trial because he deserves it.

When they reached the stairs connecting the court of the temple with the fortress, the soldiers carried Paul to save him from the violence of the crowds who were following him, crying out and demanding his death.

entries.section: (4) Paul in the custody of the Roman government

paragraphs.text: When they were about to enter the fortress, Paul spoke to the commander in Greek, asking permission to speak with him. The commander was amazed at his knowledge of Greek, and felt that he was of a high degree of culture, for he had supposed him to be a Jew who knew only Aramaic or Hebrew, which is the language of the Jews.

entries.section: (4) Paul in the custody of the Roman government

paragraphs.text: An Egyptian had led a band of robbers and murderers to Jerusalem, and claimed to be a prophet, and the number of his followers reached thirty thousand. He persuaded them that if he stood with them on the Mount of Olives opposite Jerusalem and commanded the walls of Jerusalem to fall, they would fall, and he would lead them to plunder the city. Felix the governor fought them and killed four hundred of them and captured two hundred, then the Egyptian fled and his army was scattered in A.D. 54. The commander supposed that Paul was this man who was wanted for arrest.

entries.section: (4) Paul in the custody of the Roman government

paragraphs.text: Paul told him that he was a citizen of the well-known city of Tarsus, and that he was a Jew and not an Egyptian, but from the region of Cilicia, which is part of present-day Turkey, and asked him to permit him to address the crowds.

entries.section: (4) Paul in the custody of the Roman government

paragraphs.text: The commander permitted Paul, so he stood on the stairs and beckoned with his hand, and the people became completely quiet, and he began to address them in the Hebrew language to win their goodwill.

God sends to His children someone to deliver them at the right time from the hand of those who wrong them, and preserves their lives to complete their mission, as He did with Paul. So be reassured, continue your life in positive works, and do not worry about the threats of the wicked.
Paul's address to the Jews in the temple

entries.section: (1) Paul's vision on the road to Damascus

paragraphs.text: Paul began his defense of himself by showing great respect to those who had beaten him, calling them brethren and fathers, pointing to his Jewish origin and his respect for his elders despite their wrong toward him, and he asked them to listen to his defense of himself.

entries.section: (1) Paul's vision on the road to Damascus

paragraphs.text: Paul used the Hebrew language in his speech to win their sympathy, and he succeeded in making them silent to listen to him, because they thought he would address them in Greek, which they also understood, but he spoke in the national language to show his attachment to his Jewish life and to the Law, and so he attracted their attention and their listening.

entries.section: (1) Paul's vision on the road to Damascus

paragraphs.text: At the feet: the custom anciently was for the teacher to sit on a seat and the disciples before him on the ground.
The perfect manner of the law: the study of the Law with all exactness.
Of the fathers: handed down from the fathers.
Zealous: holding fast to the law of God with zeal and care.

Paul began to tell of his former life as a Jew born in Tarsus in Turkey, but was sent to study the Law in Jerusalem, and became a disciple at the hands of Gamaliel, the famous Jewish teacher, whom everyone respected for the breadth of his understanding and the moderation of his thought, and who was one of the seventy elders of the highest council of the Jews, that is, the Sanhedrin. In Jerusalem he learned and trained to carry out the Law with all zeal and exactness.

entries.section: (1) Paul's vision on the road to Damascus

paragraphs.text: Paul persecuted Christianity when it appeared, and Christianity was called "the Way," because its children considered it the way to reach God, and we do not forget the saying of the Lord Christ, "I am the way" (Jn 14:6). He used to seize the Christians, men and women, with all cruelty, and bind them and lead them to prison and death; indeed it was he who stood to keep the garments of those who stoned Stephen.

entries.section: (1) Paul's vision on the road to Damascus

paragraphs.text: Paul called to witness the high priest and the members of the highest council, because they had previously given him letters to the synagogue of the Jews in Damascus, so that he might seize those of the Jews who had become Christians and bring them to Jerusalem to be tried and punished.

entries.section: (1) Paul's vision on the road to Damascus

paragraphs.text: Paul declared the reason for his change from persecuting Christianity to believing in it, which was a divine revelation to him from heaven. While he was on the way to Damascus, a vision appeared to him at noon, in which he saw a great light.

entries.section: (1) Paul's vision on the road to Damascus

paragraphs.text: Paul fell to the ground and heard the voice of Christ rebuking him because of his persecution of Him, for his persecution of the Christians is a persecution of Christ Himself.

entries.section: (1) Paul's vision on the road to Damascus

paragraphs.text: When Paul asked the speaker who He was, He answered that He is Jesus Christ whom Paul was persecuting.

entries.section: (1) Paul's vision on the road to Damascus

paragraphs.text: Those who were with Paul, of the Jews, testify that they saw the light and were afraid, but although they heard the voice they did not understand the words.

And we notice that there is no real difference between what Paul mentioned here and what is mentioned in the same book in the ninth chapter in the description of the vision. Of those with Paul it was said that they heard the voice and saw no one, that is, they heard a sound without understanding the words clearly and in detail. And they saw the light but did not distinguish in it a particular person, and this agrees with what is stated here. So there is no difference between the two texts.

entries.section: (1) Paul's vision on the road to Damascus

paragraphs.text: Christ asked Paul to enter Damascus, where God had arranged for him what he would do for the rest of his life.

entries.section: (1) Paul's vision on the road to Damascus

paragraphs.text: Since he lost his sight for a temporary period because of the brightness of the light, his companions led him the rest of the way to Damascus.

If you sin unintentionally, God's grace does not reject you but guides you to repentance and return to Him. So be obedient to the voice of God, and you will enjoy His care and He will be glorified in you and through you.

Paul told that Ananias, a man exact in keeping the Law and whose piety all testify to, a Jew who had become a Christian and indeed had become a priest, came and prayed, and his sight returned to him at once.
That thou shouldest know his will: the Christian teachings and the salvation that Christ accomplished on the Cross. That Just One: Christ.

Of his mouth: the direct teachings from Christ in his solitude with Him for three years in the wilderness. The Apostle declared that Christ had chosen him to see Him and hear His voice, therefore the Church considers Paul an apostle like the twelve apostles, because he heard the call from the Lord and spoke with Him as they did, when he was alone with Him three years in the wilderness (Gal 1:17-18).
After this vision and his solitude with Christ in the wilderness, Paul was to witness for Him and preach Him among the Jews and the Gentiles.

Ananias asked Paul to hasten to receive Baptism for the forgiveness of his sins. This shows that Baptism is a sacrament of the Church and not ordinary water, because it forgives sins. He also asked him to pray, calling on the name of Christ as God, for the rite of Baptism includes the declaration of faith in Christ by the one being baptized.

It is a great grace to know Christ and be joined to the Church. So take care to deepen your knowledge of God in His Church and submit to His will which He declares to you in His Holy Book and at the hand of your father of confession. And take care to teach and draw others to enjoy with you the fellowship of God in the Church.

entries.section: (3) Paul's vision in the temple and the agitation of the Jews against him

paragraphs.text: Paul returned from Damascus to Jerusalem after about three years that he spent in the Arabian desert adjoining Damascus, in which he received the faith from Christ Himself as an apostle (1 Cor 11:23). While he was praying in the temple, he fell into a trance. He declares here that his becoming a Christian had not removed him from praying in the temple or from holding fast to the promises of God to the fathers and their teachings, so as to win the Jews and his hearers when they see that he is still like them.

entries.section: (3) Paul's vision in the temple and the agitation of the Jews against him

paragraphs.text: He saw Christ in a vision, asking him to leave Jerusalem quickly, since its people would not receive his testimony.

entries.section: (3) Paul's vision in the temple and the agitation of the Jews against him

paragraphs.text: Paul thought that his past, which they knew, in his persecution of Christianity, would be a motive for them to accept his testimony, and especially his part in the killing of Stephen, the chief of the deacons and the first martyr, and his complete consent to that killing by keeping the garments of those who stoned him. If he was so great a persecutor of Christianity, then his change and conviction of it must have been for strong and convincing reasons, which would make the Jews accept his words and be affected by them.

entries.section: (3) Paul's vision in the temple and the agitation of the Jews against him

paragraphs.text: Christ sent Paul to preach among the Gentiles, far from Jerusalem and the nation of the Jews. This means that Paul's preaching to the Gentiles is a divine command and is not against the Jews nor a neglect of the teaching of the fathers.

entries.section: (3) Paul's vision in the temple and the agitation of the Jews against him

paragraphs.text: Here the Jews were greatly enraged because he considered the Gentiles better than themselves, and they demanded of the commander that he be killed, since they believed that salvation is for the Jews only and despised the Gentiles, and did not understand the prophecies of the prophets about the faith of the Gentiles and their salvation.

entries.section: (3) Paul's vision in the temple and the agitation of the Jews against him

paragraphs.text: The Jews began to shout, expressing the intensity of their anger against him, and cast off their clothes and threw them down as if preparing to stone him, so that they would not hinder the movement of their hands in stoning. And they threw dust into the air instead of throwing stones at Paul, since the commander prevented them from that, and they did not know that they were rejecting the opportunity of their believing through Paul's preaching, which perhaps was the last, just as they had earlier rejected the visitation of Christ to Jerusalem when He wept over it (Lk 19:41).

entries.section: (3) Paul's vision in the temple and the agitation of the Jews against him

paragraphs.text: The commander ordered the speech to be ended and that he be taken into the fortress and tortured by beating, so that he might confess what evil he had done that made the Jews hate him so, especially since the commander did not know the Hebrew language in which Paul had delivered his speech.

It is good for a person to discern the voice of God and not reject it as these did, for this may be the last opportunity for repentance, and after it comes hardness of heart through sin. So examine yourself by every word God sends you and review yourself every day before you sleep, so that if you have rushed into anger or contempt and rejected the word of God, you may return and submit to it and repent.

When they bound Paul in preparation for scourging him, he said to the centurion whom the commander had charged with supervising that, that he was a Roman by nationality and it was not permitted to scourge him. So the centurion hurried and told the commander this, because whoever scourges a Roman is punished by death according to Roman law.

The commander came at once to Paul, and made sure from him personally that he was a Roman, since the punishment of one who claims this falsely is death; and he marvelled that he had this privilege, for he had supposed him to be an ordinary Jew.

The commander told Paul that he had bought this rank, since the Caesars used to sell it and it was a source of great income to them, and asked Paul how he obtained the honor of this citizenship, and Paul declared that he had it by inheritance from his father and his forefathers, and this is considered a higher degree than that which is purchased.
The commander was afraid at once because he had been hasty in binding Paul for scourging, and he removed from him those who were about to scourge him.

The next day the commander ordered the chief priests and the council of the Sanhedrin to be gathered, and brought Paul down from the fortress to the council, and Paul stood to be tried before the council of which he had been a member, and the commander himself attended to know what Paul had done.

It is your right to defend yourself and use your means, but let it be for the glory of God and not for personal purposes. At the same time, do not be disturbed if you find no opportunity to defend yourself. And accept sufferings for the sake of Christ, taking care that you are not at fault in anything, that is, that you suffer while innocent, and thus you will have the heavenly reward.
Paul's address in the Sanhedrin, the plot of the Jews, and his transfer to Caesarea

entries.section: (1) The failure of the first trial

paragraphs.text: Earnestly beholding: looking intently.

Paul looked intently at these men, among whom he had been a member twenty-five years before, trying Stephen for the same reason for which they were now trying him. Did they know him? And did he know some of them? He called them brethren because he was a member like them in the council of the seventy, and he made clear to them that he had lived serving God with faithfulness when he was a Jew and also after he became a Christian.

entries.section: (1) The failure of the first trial

paragraphs.text: Ananias: he was the high priest, a Sadducee, unjust and covetous of the portions of the lesser priests, and was greatly hated.

Ananias commanded his attendants to strike Paul on the mouth because he showed his sincerity and righteousness, which showed that the members of the council were mistaken in their accusation of him, and this striking meant contempt and mockery of Paul.

entries.section: (1) The failure of the first trial

paragraphs.text: Paul prophesied about Ananias, saying that God would smite him because he is a hypocritical man, like a wall that is bad inside but whose outside is fair to look at. This prophecy was fulfilled after 5 years, when a rebellion was plotted against him under the leadership of his son, and he fled and hid, but they found him and killed him. Paul rebuked him for commanding that he be struck, as if he were guilty, before his trial, and this is against the law, which gives every person the opportunity to defend himself first.

entries.section: (1) The failure of the first trial

paragraphs.text: When those near Ananias rebuked him, he said that he did not know that Ananias was the high priest, because the Jews and the Romans used to depose high priests often and appoint others, contrary to the law, which appointed the high priest for all the days of his life.

And there was nothing to prove that Ananias was of the descendants of Aaron so as to be high priest. Paul had left the Jewish councils a long time before, so he no longer knew the present high priest, especially since many of those sitting were former high priests, and the high priest had no distinctive clothing outside the service. Paul declared his knowledge of the law (Ex 22:28), which provides that the high priest is not to be reviled; so he was not violating the law, because he did not know that Ananias was high priest.

entries.section: (1) The failure of the first trial

paragraphs.text: When Paul looked intently at them, he knew that some of them were Pharisees, who believe in spirits and the resurrection, and others were Sadducees, who do not believe in that, but hold that the soul dies with the body and does not rise. So the Holy Spirit guided Paul and he declared that he was of the party of the Pharisees, as was his father, that is, he had lived all his Jewish life as a Pharisee and believes in the resurrection of the dead, which the fathers believe and the Pharisees hold. He said this out of despair of a just judgment of the council upon him, and perhaps by this he might draw the Pharisees to faith in Christ.

entries.section: (1) The failure of the first trial

paragraphs.text: Although the Sadducees accept the five books of Moses, they do not believe in the resurrection of the dead, nor in the existence of angels, although these are mentioned in those books, for they hold that these angels were created by God for divine purposes in the service of men and then vanished afterward. So when the Pharisees heard that Paul was a Pharisee, they sided with him because he believes as they do against the Sadducees, and here a dissension arose, indeed a dispute, between the two parties over Paul and the accusations directed against him.

entries.section: (1) The failure of the first trial

paragraphs.text: Most of the scribes were Pharisees and some were Sadducees, and the chief difference between the Pharisees and the Sadducees is belief in the resurrection and immortality. When Paul proclaimed the resurrection of the dead, the Pharisees felt that he was like them, and considered the accusations against him small, so they neglected them and defended him, and regarded the vision which he related to them, of the appearance of Christ to him, as an angel that had appeared to him and called him to preach to the Gentiles. They did not object to that, for what was most important in their view was to oppose the Sadducees, who do not believe in the resurrection.

Thus their orators and scribes cried out in defense of Paul. This does not mean that they believed in Christ, but was merely partisanship for their belief in the resurrection against the Sadducees, because they considered Christ merely a spirit or an angel.

entries.section: (1) The failure of the first trial

paragraphs.text: The commander feared that they would attack Paul and tear him in pieces because of the contention of the two parties to pull him, each to its own side, the Pharisees to protect him and the Sadducees to take vengeance on him, so he commanded the soldiers to take him back to the fortress.

entries.section: (1) The failure of the first trial

paragraphs.text: The following night, the Lord appeared to Paul to reassure and encourage him, and also to tell him that he would go to preach in Rome according to the desire of his heart. This shows that what Paul said to the high priest was not a fault or anger, but a witness to Christ which He welcomed and encouraged him to continue.

The high priest Ananias was a bad example who made people turn away from his religion when they saw him, while Paul, by the purity of his conduct, was a witness to people for his religion. With which of the two parties does each of us stand? Know that your words and actions are noticed by those around you and they follow them. You are the image of Christ; do not turn away from it lest you become a curse to His name, and be confident that example through your behavior is far better than preaching and teaching without practice.

entries.section: (2) The plot and the transfer to Caesarea

paragraphs.text: In the morning, some of the fanatical Jews who were agitated against Paul, of the sect of the Sadducees, agreed together that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.

entries.section: (2) The plot and the transfer to Caesarea

paragraphs.text: The agitators, who numbered more than forty persons, announced to the chief priests and elders of the Jews their fast from food and drink until they killed Paul. This confirms their insistence on that, and also shows the evil into which the leaders of the Jewish nation had fallen and their determination to kill a man who had not been tried or given an opportunity to defend himself.

entries.section: (2) The plot and the transfer to Caesarea

paragraphs.text: The agitators were unable to storm the barracks to kill Paul, so they asked the Jewish leaders, who had again agreed on killing Paul after having differed in the council, to request the commander to bring Paul down for his case to be retried and examined, and on the way the agitators would kill him, and thus no charge would be brought against the chief priests.

entries.section: (2) The plot and the transfer to Caesarea

paragraphs.text: Because the agreement to kill Paul was among a large number, the news leaked to some of the Jews, and the agitators were careful to hide the matter only from the commander, for they did not expect that one of Paul's relatives would be among them, but God permitted Paul's sister's son to be in Jerusalem, and he heard of the plot, so he entered the barracks as a friend of Paul wishing to visit him in the fortress and told him of the matter.

entries.section: (2) The plot and the transfer to Caesarea

paragraphs.text: Paul sent his sister's son with a centurion to the commander to tell him of the plot, and this shows the importance of a person exerting all his effort for his own salvation, and not relying passively on God's promise of deliverance, as Christ declared to Paul in the vision, that He would deliver him and that he would witness in Rome also.

entries.section: (2) The plot and the transfer to Caesarea

paragraphs.text: The centurion told the commander that Paul had called him and asked that this young man be brought to the commander to tell him important matters, so the commander was gracious to Paul's sister's son and asked him privately what news he had.

entries.section: (2) The plot and the transfer to Caesarea

paragraphs.text: The young man told the commander of the plot of the Jews to kill Paul, asking him not to agree to their request to bring Paul down to them.

entries.section: (2) The plot and the transfer to Caesarea

paragraphs.text: The commander asked him not to tell anyone, lest they take vengeance on him.

entries.section: (2) The plot and the transfer to Caesarea

paragraphs.text: Caesarea: the seat of the Roman authority in this region, 70 miles from Jerusalem. By the grace of God, the commander believed the young man's words and was concerned to save Paul, so he asked two of his officers to prepare 470 armed soldiers to take Paul to Caesarea at the third hour of the night, that is, nine in the evening by present reckoning, the time when the streets and traffic are quiet.

entries.section: (2) The plot and the transfer to Caesarea

paragraphs.text: The commander commanded that Paul be mounted and sent under the guard of the soldiers to Felix the Roman at Caesarea.

entries.section: (2) The plot and the transfer to Caesarea

paragraphs.text: The commander sent a letter to the governor, the text of which St. Luke published.

entries.section: (2) The plot and the transfer to Caesarea

paragraphs.text: The commander, whose name was Claudius Lysias, sent his greetings to the governor Felix, and informed him that Paul was a Roman by nationality, and that he had rescued him from the hands of the Jews who had seized him, and noticed during his trial before the Jews that the dispute between him and them was religious and not political, and there was no charge against him for which Roman law would hold him accountable.

entries.section: (2) The plot and the transfer to Caesarea

paragraphs.text: When the commander learned of the plot of the Jews to kill Paul, he hastened to send him to the governor at Caesarea so that the trial might take place there.

entries.section: (2) The plot and the transfer to Caesarea

paragraphs.text: The soldiers marched all night until they reached the city of Antipatris, having covered two-thirds of the distance to Caesarea.

entries.section: (2) The plot and the transfer to Caesarea

paragraphs.text: When morning came, the foot soldiers returned to Jerusalem and left with him the horsemen, who completed the road with him to Caesarea, and delivered him and the letter to the governor.

entries.section: (2) The plot and the transfer to Caesarea

paragraphs.text: The governor inquired of what province Paul was, perhaps to make sure from the records of Cilicia that his citizenship was Roman, or to learn something from his city that would help him regarding the charges against him, or to send him to his city if it was near, to be tried there, if he wished to be rid of him.

entries.section: (2) The plot and the transfer to Caesarea

paragraphs.text: Felix told Paul that he would hold a lawful trial when his accusers came from Jerusalem, and he kept Paul in custody pending investigation in the great palace of Herod at Caesarea.

God's arrangements for the deliverance of His children are very wonderful, for He preserved Paul from evil, and helped him to complete his mission so that he might witness to Christ in Rome. So He works with us when we commit our affairs to Him. Do not be disturbed by the plots of the wicked, for God gives you favor in the eyes of those in authority over you, and delivers you in wonderful ways until you fulfill His will.
Paul's continuing as a prisoner until the end of Felix's governorship. Felix had been a slave and was freed, and he was wicked, corrupt and covetous, as will be shown by his later treatment of Paul.

After five days Ananias the high priest came with some elders of the Jews, as delegates of the Sanhedrin, and Ananias was full of evil and hatred toward Paul because he had been rebuked by him. He brought with him a Roman advocate named Tertullus, and they began to present their complaint against Paul.
They brought Paul for the trial, and the advocate began to plead.

Tertullus praised Felix the governor, declaring that the Jewish nation, on whose behalf Tertullus was speaking, enjoyed security because of the justice of his rule, for he had arrested the gangs that committed robbery and murder, and quelled many rebellions, and therefore they thanked him. Although Felix, on the other hand, was characterized by cruelty, injustice and immersion in licentiousness, for he killed Jonathan, the high priest of the Jews, secretly; and the Jews brought a suit against him before the Romans which led to his removal two years after the date of this plea.

Tertullus said wisely that he did not wish to expand in describing the virtues of Felix lest he hinder his precious time, and asked humbly that he hear him, as a representative of the Jews, in his clemency. This shows his skill as an orator in persuading and winning the affection of his hearers.
The Nazarenes: a contemptuous name for the followers of Christ, since Nazareth was a small town in Galilee, which was full of pagan Gentiles.
Tertullus accused Paul of three charges, and considered him a corrupter and harmful to society, and these charges are:
1- That he is a man who corrupts the people and stirs up sedition and discord among all the Jews of the world.
2- That he was not content with creating problems, but led a group which he called the Nazarenes.

3- The third charge with which Tertullus accused Paul was his profaning of the temple by bringing Trophimus the Ephesian, a Gentile, into a place which Gentiles may not enter. This did not happen, but was merely a supposition and claim of the Jews, and the Jews wanted to try him according to the law on these three charges.

Tertullus added that the commander Lysias had taken him from them with great violence, and by this he directed blame at the commander for being unjust and said that they had wished to try him justly, while it was they who had been beating Paul with all violence with the intent to kill him.

Tertullus continued his speech, accusing the commander Lysias not only of preventing them from trying Paul, but also of burdening them with the hardship of travelling to Caesarea to plead before Felix the governor. And he told the governor that he could make sure of their complaint by questioning the commander and examining Paul, and the Jews agreed to everything Tertullus said.

Paul answered, when he was permitted to speak, that he was glad that Felix had governed the Jews for about 6 years, that is, since A.D. 52, because by that he would have come to know the wickedness of the character of the Jews and their cunning.
Paul defended himself in two ways:
1- That he had come up to Jerusalem only twelve days before, and had spent most of them in confinement because of the Jews.

2- That he had come to practice worship in the temple as a Jew, for Paul considered Christianity an extension of Judaism and its completion, so he cares for worship in the temple and is not a defiler of it as they accused him.

Paul denied their accusation against him that he was a stirrer-up of sedition, as proved by the fact that they had not seized him in the temple disputing or stirring up those present, nor in the synagogues of Jerusalem nor its streets.

Paul answered the charge of stirring up sedition and also his profaning of the temple, and showed that they were false charges. As for the third charge, that he was a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes, he declared that he was indeed of the Nazarenes, that is, a Christian, but he made clear that Christianity does not conflict with Judaism but is its completion. For he believes in the God whom the Jews worship, and also believes in the Law and the prophets, and since the Romans recognized Judaism as a religion and Christianity as a sect of it, there was no legal accusation in that.

Paul affirmed that as a Christian he believes Judaism, not only in the one God and the Law and the prophets, but he also has hope in the general resurrection like the faith of the Jews. And we notice that the resurrection is for all, righteous and wicked.
Paul declared that he strives to have a conscience void of offence before God and to cause no one to stumble.

Paul came after his absence from Jerusalem for many years, to offer sacrifices and worship at the feast of Pentecost, and to present alms to the Jews which he had collected from the churches of the Gentiles in which he had preached.

The Jews found Paul in the temple with the Asian Jews, that is, the Turks, performing the duties of purification according to the law and offering sacrifices, and they did not find him making a riot; this is his answer to their accusation of him of stirring up sedition. In spite of that, the Jews accused him of having been with Gentiles in the temple, and this of course did not happen. And these Asian Jews, his companions in the temple, did not attend this session of the trial to give their statements and present their complaint if there was anything against him; they are witnesses who could be consulted.

The Jews present had tried him in Jerusalem before their council, and had found no fault in him except that he believes in the resurrection of the dead, which the Pharisees supported and the Sadducees objected to.

Paul thereby seized the opportunity to preach to those who were trying him and to Felix himself his faith in Christ the Savior who rose from the dead, because Paul's mission as a servant was the most important aim in his life, so he turned every situation into an opportunity for ministry. Would that you seize every opportunity to show Christ through your love and your good conduct and kind words, and do not fear anyone, because God supports you in all the situations of your life.

The Jews wanted an immediate judgment from Felix against Paul, but he had some knowledge of Christianity, so he asked them to wait until the commander Lysias came down to Caesarea from Jerusalem and he heard his testimony, because they had cited him in their pleading, and perhaps he was not convinced by their accusations but did not wish to anger them, so he postponed the judgment and left it pending, seeing that Paul was innocent.

He commanded the centurion to keep Paul in custody and fix his residence in a specified place without restraints, with permission for him to meet his friends. This shows his conviction of Paul's innocence, but he aimed at pleasing the Jews or at obtaining a bribe from Paul.
It seems that Drusilla, Felix's wife, who was a Jewess, asked her husband to see and hear Paul. So he sent for him from his confinement, and he spoke about faith in Christ.

Paul spoke about holiness, chastity and the day of judgment, and Felix trembled at that because of his many sins and his fear of judgment, and postponed the rest of the talk to another meeting. And we notice that Drusilla did not tremble at Paul's talk, because she thought that her Judaism and outward religiousness would save her from judgment.

Since Felix had heard that Paul had brought with him money for alms for the Christians of Jerusalem, he hoped that Paul would give him a bribe from it to release him, so he repeated his meetings with him, but Paul did not give him any, because of his confidence in his own innocence.
Paul remained in custody for two years, until Rome summoned Felix to investigate the complaint of the Jews against him, and Festus came as governor in place of Felix in A.D. 60.

And Felix wished to soften his relations with the Jews so that they would withdraw their complaint against him, so he did not release Paul before handing over the governorship to Festus, but left him in his confinement.

God turns everything to good for His children. Felix did not know that this action would be the cause of Paul's travelling at the state's expense to Rome, the capital, to be tried there, and to preach in Rome in the name of Christ as he had often wished.
So accept God's arrangements even if they are contrary to your will, because God loves you and arranges good for you. Paul before Festus and his appeal to Caesar

Festus took over the governorship of Palestine, whose seat was Caesarea. He remained in the governorship two years, and was a just man. Because Jerusalem is the largest city of his province, he went up to it three days after taking over the governorship in Caesarea.
The chief of the Jews: the members of their highest council, that is, the Sanhedrin.
Desired favour against him: asking that he grant them a favor and be gracious to them by accepting their complaint and renewing the trial of Paul.

In Jerusalem, the Jews renewed their complaint to Festus against Paul through their high priest and the members of the Sanhedrin, and asked him to do them a service by bringing Paul to Jerusalem to try him there. Sadly, they had secretly plotted to kill him on the road from Caesarea to Jerusalem, as they had plotted before.
Festus did not agree, because he was about to go to Caesarea quickly, and he commanded that Paul be kept in Caesarea. This was by God's arrangement to protect Paul.
Festus asked the Jews to send down with him a delegation representing them to bring the case in Caesarea.
Festus stayed ten days in Jerusalem, then came to Caesarea and began to try Paul the day after his return. This shows his activity and his justice.
They brought Paul, and the Jews began to make many complaints against him with religious and civil charges, grave and false, which they were not able to prove.

Paul's defense centered on the fact that he was innocent of any charge against the Law, or the temple, or Caesar. These are the same three accusations that had been directed against him two years earlier before Felix the governor (ch. 24:5-6).
To do the Jews a pleasure: to be gracious to them and appease them and give them a gift, which was the trial of Paul in Jerusalem as they requested.

Because of the pressure of the Jews on Festus to resume the trial in Jerusalem, he tried to appease them. On the other hand, since he saw Paul's innocence, he asked him whether he wished to be tried in Jerusalem so as to obtain a civil and religious acquittal. Here the justice of Festus appears in two matters:
1- That the religious trial in Jerusalem would take place in the presence of Festus, to keep him safe from any injustice.
2- That he asked him whether he wished to go to Jerusalem or not.

Since Paul knew the cunning and tricks of the Jews, he protested that he was in the official court of the capital of Palestine at Caesarea, and that he was innocent, as the governor knew. In this he used his civil right as a Roman to nullify the deceit and evil of the Jews, especially since he was innocent by the testimony of the governor himself after his trials before him.

Paul declared that he was not asking for his acquittal as a gift from anyone, but that he was in fact innocent. How then could the governor hand him over to their counsel to kill him? He also declared his appeal of the case to the court of Caesar in Rome. This was his right as a Roman in such circumstances.

Festus suspended the hearing of the case as a formal procedure, and consulted his counselors, who recommended accepting Paul's request because it was lawful. So Festus declared to Paul that his appeal was accepted, and that he would go to the court of Caesar in Rome as he had requested.

St. Paul did not lose an opportunity to spread the ministry, even in Rome the capital. His personal case did not occupy his thought, but how he might go to Rome to preach in it. This is the true servant who counts nothing until he fulfills his ministry (ch. 20:24). Seize every opportunity to show Christ through your words and actions, and offer love to everyone you meet, and thus you show Christ to all.

entries.section: (2) The meeting of Festus and Agrippa

paragraphs.text: Agrippa: a ruler over regions next to Judea, the son of the Herod whom the angel of the Lord smote with worms and who died in A.D. 44 after he had killed the Apostle James the Great. Agrippa was king over some regions adjoining Judea, and he showed his interest in the Jewish religion, but he betrayed the Jews at the destruction of Jerusalem.
Bernice: Agrippa's sister, who lived with him in adultery after her widowhood.
Agrippa and his sister Bernice came to greet Festus and congratulate him on the new governorship.

entries.section: (2) The meeting of Festus and Agrippa

paragraphs.text: Their visit was prolonged, so Festus laid before them the matter of Paul, who had been in custody since the days of the previous governor Felix.

entries.section: (2) The meeting of Festus and Agrippa

paragraphs.text: The chief of the Jews and their priests tried to obtain a sentence of condemnation against him.

entries.section: (2) The meeting of Festus and Agrippa

paragraphs.text: Festus adhered to Roman law, which forbids a death sentence without trial and defense.

entries.section: (2) The meeting of Festus and Agrippa

paragraphs.text: When the Jews came to Caesarea and Festus tried him face to face with them, they were not able to prove their accusations, and Festus found no crime in him against Roman law.

entries.section: (2) The meeting of Festus and Agrippa

paragraphs.text: Festus informed Agrippa that the disputes between the Jews and Paul were religious, and they differed about a person called Jesus, whom the Jews said was dead, but Paul said was alive.

entries.section: (2) The meeting of Festus and Agrippa

paragraphs.text: Because of this Festus was hesitant whether to release him or not. For he was innocent civilly, and so he asked him whether he wished to be tried religiously in the synagogue council of Jerusalem to obtain religious acquittal also.

entries.section: (2) The meeting of Festus and Agrippa

paragraphs.text: Paul refused to go to Jerusalem, and appealed his case to Caesar, who was entitled "Augustus," that is, the one revered with the reverence due to gods. Thus it became necessary to send him to Caesar.

entries.section: (2) The meeting of Festus and Agrippa

paragraphs.text: Agrippa asked to hear Paul out of his longing to hear more about Christianity, and Festus promised him that he would let him hear him the next day.

Perhaps God wished to give Agrippa and his sister the opportunity of hearing the preaching and repentance so that they might repent. For God seeks the repentance of all His children, whatever their conduct, but how many important opportunities like this one a person loses!
So know that every spiritual word or guidance you hear in the Church or outside it is a personal message for you to apply in your life, and not a general sermon concerning others.
Chief captains: they are the commanders of thousands of Roman soldiers.

Festus held a great celebration for Agrippa, who came with Bernice, and at the celebration were the chief commanders of the army with the great men of the city, then they brought Paul to the hall of audience.
Festus opened the session by presenting Paul, whom the Jews had sought by every means to kill in Jerusalem and Caesarea.
Although he had found nothing in his deeds deserving death, yet because Paul had appealed to Caesar, Festus agreed to send him to him.

Festus had found no specific charge to write in the letter referring the case to Caesar, whom he called "my lord," and perhaps this session would help him determine the charges, especially since King Agrippa knows Judaism well, so Festus would find what to write.
Festus made clear that it is folly to refer a case to the emperor without a reason, otherwise this would show his incompetence as a governor in examining cases.
God was still alerting Festus to faith through the words and case of Paul, whose innocence appears clearly. For God seeks the salvation of all.

Thus this council is the fifth defense since the arrest of Paul in Jerusalem: the first was before the crowds of the Jews in the temple, the second before the council of the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem, the third before Felix in Caesarea, the fourth before Festus in Caesarea, and the fifth, this one, before King Agrippa and Festus in Caesarea. And through all this Paul was innocent by the testimony of those who tried him.

We must not be surprised if the showing of our innocence is delayed. For to everything under heaven there is a time, and we are not greater or more righteous than the great Apostle Paul. So accept being accused falsely, and if you defend yourself and they do not hear you, do not be disturbed, knowing that your endurance is very precious in God's sight and He rewards you for it, and He is able at the right time to show your innocence.
Paul's defense before Agrippa
Agrippa, as president of the celebration, permitted Paul to begin presenting his point of view.
So Paul stretched forth his hand, bound with the chain, and began by saying that he was happy to be tried before a king who knows Judaism and is able to understand his religious point of view.

Paul made clear that King Agrippa knows the details of the Jewish religion, so that some supposed that he had become a Jew; therefore he would explain to him in some detail, because the Roman governors do not care about matters of Jewish worship.

The most straitest sect of our religion: the Pharisees were famous for the literal exactness of the Law and the setting down of many rules for that, with neglect of the spiritual meaning, so worship was emptied of its depth and became a constraint on people in their conduct.

Paul made clear that he grew up a Jew, and was brought up in Jerusalem to study the Law and was well known for that, and that he lived as a follower of the sect of the Pharisees, strict in the rites and the keeping of the commandments.
The hope of the promise: of the expected Messiah who will save His people and redeem them by His death and then His resurrection.
Our twelve tribes: all the Jews.

Paul declared his faith in eternal life and the resurrection from the dead, which was accomplished in Christ the expected Messiah. He linked the faith of the Jews in the Messiah with the resurrection of this Messiah from the dead, so he believes in the Messiah like the Jews, and this faith of theirs is the aim of their continual worship night and day, and consequently there is no need to try him, because he agrees with them in faith in the Messiah.

Paul asks why it should be hard for a Jew to believe the resurrection of the dead in general and of Christ in particular. Did not the Old Testament mention several times the raising of the dead by Elijah and Elisha?
Paul mentions that when he was a Jew, he was determined to oppose Christ and Christianity, because he supposed it to be foreign to Judaism and did not understand that it is its completion.

Paul acknowledged his persecution of the Christians in Jerusalem as all the Jews know, using the authority of the chief priests to imprison and kill many of the Jews who had become Christians, since he was a member of the Sanhedrin, and at the end of the trial of each, the members cast lots to make sure of his condemnation or innocence before killing him, and Paul took part in that also, and the casting of votes was done mostly by voting and the majority of opinions.

Paul's activity extended to the synagogues of Jerusalem, Judea and elsewhere, so he sentenced the Christians to beating and scourging until they would deny the name of Christ, and he was furious against them and drove them out beyond the province of Judea.

Paul wronged Christ supposing that this was the truth. So do not rush in your actions, but review yourself and listen to the counsel of guides lest you wrong the innocent or declare mistaken opinions.

entries.section: (2) The vision and the change of life

paragraphs.text: Paul acknowledges that on one occasion he was going to Damascus with letters and commissions from the chief priests to seize the Christians and kill them.

entries.section: (2) The vision and the change of life

paragraphs.text: Here Paul tells for the third time of Christ's meeting with him on the way to Damascus (ch. 9:3, 22:6). On the way at noon, he saw a light from heaven, above the brightness of the noonday sun, shining round about him and those with him, as happened at the Transfiguration.

entries.section: (2) The vision and the change of life

paragraphs.text: They all fell to the earth in fear, and a voice spoke to him saying in Hebrew, "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" and made clear to him that his persecuting stance would not benefit him but would harm him, and likened his work to an ox kicking against iron goads (pricks).

entries.section: (2) The vision and the change of life

paragraphs.text: Paul asked the speaker who He was, and He answered that He is Jesus whom he and his followers were persecuting.

entries.section: (2) The vision and the change of life

paragraphs.text: Christ asked Paul to stand up and made clear to him that He had not appeared to him to punish him, but, as Ananias informed him afterward, that the Lord had chosen him to serve His name and witness to his faith, according to what he saw in the vision and what would appear to him afterward.

entries.section: (2) The vision and the change of life

paragraphs.text: The people: the Jews.
The Gentiles: this is an explanation before Agrippa, that he did not go to the Gentiles of himself but God sent him, and if this troubled the Jews it was because they hate the Gentiles.
Unto whom now I send thee: this confirms that Paul is an apostle from God.
God promised Paul that He would deliver him from the Jews and the Gentiles among whom he would serve, until he completed his ministry and at the end was martyred.

entries.section: (2) The vision and the change of life

paragraphs.text: Paul declared that his preaching would open the eyes of those far off, that they might return to God from the darkness of sin and be freed from slavery to the devil and become children of God. And they would believe in the name of the Lord, and their sins would be forgiven them and they would receive a heavenly inheritance with the saints.

entries.section: (2) The vision and the change of life

paragraphs.text: Paul determined to obey Christ who appeared to him in the vision, so he preached in His name in Damascus, where he was baptized, and in Jerusalem and all the region of Judea, and then to the Gentiles also, to call them to repentance and return to God and to live in righteousness in good works meet for repentance and the amendment of their conduct.

entries.section: (2) The vision and the change of life

paragraphs.text: Because of Paul's preaching of the risen Christ and his preaching among the Gentiles without their needing to become Jews, the Jews seized him in the temple and wished to kill him.

entries.section: (2) The vision and the change of life

paragraphs.text: The first that should rise from the dead: Christ was not the first to rise from the dead, for many had preceded Him in the Old Testament and He Himself had raised many, but He is the first who raised Himself and went to Paradise and the Kingdom, while the others went to Hades again because Christ had not yet accomplished redemption.

Paul made clear that God preserved him as He promised, as a witness to all of what Moses and the prophets foretold of the coming of Christ and His sufferings, as in Isaiah (ch. 53), and His resurrection, as in Hosea (Hos 6:2). Thus he proclaimed the light of the Gospel to the Jews and the Gentiles.

Paul always remembered Christ's call to him to serve Him. So do not forget the aim of your life, which is to live for God and prepare for your eternity, and to declare Christ by your love, and to call all to the pure life with God.
Festus was not convinced by Paul's words, so he interrupted him, crying out and accusing him that his much reading and study had made him lose his mind.
And this is always the opinion of Satan about the children of God, and he said it through the mouth of the Jews about Christ Himself (Jn 8:48), in order to hinder the preaching.
Most noble: a title of honor given to governors and persons of high station.
Paul answered Festus respectfully, saying that he was in full possession of his senses and mind, and was speaking the truth, which is God, so that the hearers might take heed and believe.
These things: the redemption of Christ and His resurrection and the preaching of Him.
This thing was not done in a corner: it did not happen in secret, away from sight.

Paul declared to Festus that King Agrippa knows, as a Jew, all these prophecies to which Paul pointed concerning the coming of Christ and His death and resurrection, and that he had heard of the preaching of Christ and His death and resurrection in Jerusalem, and indeed had also heard of the life of Christ and His crucifixion and resurrection, which was known to all the Jews.

Paul asked Agrippa whether he believed the words of the prophets, and Paul did not wait for the answer but answered for him, saying that he believes, in order to draw him to faith and to continue hearing the preaching of Christ.

Agrippa said that Paul wanted by this little, short talk to persuade him to Christianity, whereas the subject needs long study. By this he evaded answering, otherwise he would logically be forced in the end to declare his faith in Christ.

Paul said to Agrippa that he had prayed much to God for his faith and that of the hearers, whether by few or many words of preaching, but without their suffering the pains of bonds and imprisonment. This shows Paul's zeal to preach to every person and his tenderness toward everyone who hears him, that they should not meet persecutions and bonds after believing.
The council broke up and the king and the governor rose, and everyone followed them.
Those who had gathered in the assembly departed, convinced of Paul's innocence of what he was accused of.

Agrippa affirmed Paul's innocence, and that it would have been right to set him free at the hand of Felix or Festus, but because he had appealed to Caesar, it was necessary to send him to the capital, Rome.

The longing of every Christian is to draw others to the knowledge of Christ, whom he loved and became convinced of, as Paul did here, saying, "O taste and see that the Lord is good" (Ps 34:8), for the circumstances of the Christian's life never concern him more than the success of his witness and his mission.
The voyage from Caesarea to Malta
We sail: it is understood from this that Luke accompanied Paul on this journey, and that he was also with him in Caesarea.
Augustan Regiment: it numbered 3,000 soldiers and was named after Caesar, and it served in duties attached to it.

Two years after Paul's arrest in Caesarea, Festus handed Paul and other prisoners over to a centurion named Julius, to sail with them to Italy, where the capital Rome is, so that he might be tried there.

Paul and those with him boarded a ship of Adramyttium, named after the port of Adramyttium in western Asia (Turkey), and from there they would take another ship bound for Rome. With them was Aristarchus of Macedonia (northern Greece), specifically from the city of Thessalonica, the capital of the north. The presence of Aristarchus and Luke, Paul's two disciples, with him was a great comfort to him on this journey and a proof of their great love for him in bearing the dangers of the voyage.

Courteously: perhaps this was because of Festus' recommendation, and on the other hand because of the character of Julius, and also because of Paul's gentle and attractive personality and the fact that he was a Roman.

The ship arrived at Sidon, a Phoenician city (Lebanon), sixty-seven miles north of Caesarea. Julius treated Paul kindly and permitted him to visit his friends, that is, the Christians of Sidon, so that he might receive material and moral help from them, and perhaps he seized this opportunity to preach to them and strengthen their faith.
The voyage continued westward, and they sailed under the lee of Cyprus, so that it would shield them from the opposing westerly winds.
The ship passed by the provinces of Cilicia and Pamphylia in southern Asia (Turkey), then arrived at Myra of Lycia, which is the city of Myra in southern Turkey.

In the port of Myra of Lycia, they left the ship and boarded another one coming from Egypt, from the city of Alexandria, laden with grain (wheat) (v. 38) and bound for Rome. It was a large ship that carried a great number of passengers in addition to the quantities of grain in it.

The ship was a sailing ship, and because the wind was contrary, they sailed slowly until they came near the city of Cnidus in southern Turkey. Because of the force of the northwesterly winds, they could not advance westward, so they sailed south to the island of Crete until they reached its eastern tip, where the city of Salmone is. They moved with difficulty because of the intensity of the northwesterly winds, and they passed south of Crete, which shielded them to some extent from the violence of the winds, until they came to a place called Fair Havens (a city on the southern coast of the island of Crete, near the city of Lasea).
The fast: the fast of the Day of Atonement among the Jews, which falls on the tenth of the seventh Hebrew month, in the Feast of Atonement, which occurs in the autumn.

The Jewish fast of the Day of Atonement, which falls in the autumn, had passed, and the harsh winter weather had begun, and the northwesterly winds, opposed to their course to Rome, grew strong. So Paul, by God's guidance and from his previous experience in travel, warned them that sailing at that time would bring harm to the ship, the cargo, and the passengers themselves.

The ship's pilot and its owner thought that it was possible to sail to Italy, so the centurion obeyed them and disregarded Paul's opinion, considering them more expert in the sea than Paul, who was concerned with religious and literary studies.

Because the region of Fair Havens was not suitable for wintering in, they began to look for another harbor, away from the winds, in which to spend the winter. So they tried to head the ship toward the harbor of Phenice, forty miles to the west (that is, a three-hour sail), also on the south of Crete, since the island shields them to some extent from the northwesterly winds.

A gentle south wind blew, and the sailors felt that the weather was suitable for sailing. So they moved the ship westward toward the harbor of Phenice, keeping close to the island so that the winds would not pull them out into the sea and expose them to dangers.

God often sends us His counsel, but we rely on the opinion of the world and reject God's counsel and treat it lightly, and the grave consequences become proof of the error of our conduct. So do not resist the voice of God that you hear in the Church and from your father of confession and your spiritual guides, and do not rush into your decisions, but seek God's guidance so that you are not exposed to dangers.
After they had sailed a little, about five miles westward on their way to Phenice, a storm called Euroclydon, that is, the eastern waves in Greek, rushed upon them from the northeast.
The wind seized the ship out of the sailors' control, and they were unable to face the wind, so the passengers committed themselves into God's hand, and the wind carried them wherever it willed.

They passed by the island of Clauda, trying to haul in the boat used for carrying passengers from the shore to the ship, which they had been towing behind the ship because they were nearing Phenice. But when the winds seized them, they tried to lift the boat up into the ship so that the rope tying it to the ship would not break and the boat be lost or smashed. They succeeded in this, but only after great effort because of the violence of the winds.

To meet the storms, they began to undergird the ship with strong ropes so that the wind would not pull its planks apart and water fill it. They were near a gulf in North Africa called the Syrtis, and they feared that the winds would drive them into it because it was very shallow, so that if the ship entered it, it would run aground in its bottom and the winds would break it up. So they lowered the sails to lessen the effect of the winds on the ship.
Tempest: a violent wind.
The next day, because the winds grew stronger, they threw the ship's cargo of wheat into the sea to lighten it so that its escape would be easier.
On the third day they cast the ship's furniture into the sea to lighten it further.

The rays of the sun did not appear to them because of the thickness of the clouds, and likewise the stars at night. Since guidance for finding direction in those days was not by compass but by the sun in the day and the stars at night, they lost their bearings and despaired of being saved.

Because of seasickness and great fear, they abstained from food for a long time and their bodies grew weak. Then Paul stood among them and rebuked them for not obeying him when he warned them not to set sail from Fair Havens, which exposed them to these dangers. He said this not out of pride in his own opinion and dignity, but so that they would obey him in what he would say next.
Paul announced to them the good news that none of them would be drowned, but only the ship would be wrecked.
When Paul prayed to God, He sent His angel to him in the night that had passed.
The angel told Paul not to be afraid, because he would arrive safely in Rome and stand to be tried before Caesar, and that God would save all those who sailed in the ship from drowning for his sake.

Here we compare Paul, who by his obedience to God was the cause of the salvation of the ship's passengers, with the prophet Jonah, who by his disobedience to God was the cause of a predicament for the ship's passengers, until they threw him into the sea and it grew calm for them (Jonah 1:12).
Paul declared to them his confidence in the angel's word that they would be cast upon an island. Thus Paul's obedience saved them, after their disobedience had almost destroyed them.

Whenever we obey God, He becomes a protector for us against dangers and a covering over us. So obey God's commandments and the Church's guidance even if they are against your desires, because God knows what is good for you and loves you more than you love yourself. A person does what he is convinced of, but obedience is carrying out what one is not convinced of, so it is higher than everything, and its motive is love and faith in God.
Adria: the Adriatic, beside Italy.
Shipmen: the sailors.

Fourteen days had passed on the ship since it left the island of Crete, and most of this period was tormented by the winds and exposed to destruction in the Adriatic Sea, which lies between Italy and Greece. After that, it seems the sailors heard the sound of waves breaking on a shore, so they concluded that they were near some coast, because it was night and they could see nothing.
Fathom: the length of a man, that is, about 160 cm on average.

They used a rope with a weight at its end to measure the depth of the water down to the bottom, and they found the depth to be about thirty-six meters, because a fathom is about the length of a man. Then after a while they measured again and found that the depth had decreased and was only about twenty-four meters, so they were certain that their conclusion was correct.

Anchors: the plural of anchor, which is an iron shaft with an iron arc at its end, pointed on each side. This shaft is tied by a long rope to the ship, and when this anchor is cast onto the sea bottom, it digs into it and so holds the ship in its place. It was known among sailors by the name "al-Halb." Because it was midnight and visibility was nil, they feared that the shore might be rocky, so they cast four anchors from the stern of the ship to hold the ship in its place until daylight.

The sailors planned to escape from the ship to land by means of the boat, so they began lowering it into the sea, pretending that they would lay out more anchors from the bow of the ship to secure the vessel in its place. For if they had told the truth, that they would flee in this boat, which has room only for themselves, the centurion and the soldiers would have stopped them.

Paul warned the centurion and the soldiers about the sailors' attempt to flee in the boat, since that would lead to the passengers not being saved. For God's promise of their deliverance from drowning (v. 21) does not mean that they should cease their striving to reach land.
Then the soldiers cut the ropes from which the boat hung, and it fell and was lost in the sea.

During the remainder of the night, Paul began to urge everyone in great love to eat some food, because they had eaten nothing of value for fourteen days, whether because of seasickness or fear, which had exhausted their strength, a thing that would hinder their deliverance as God had promised them, that not a hair would perish from their heads.

Here Paul appears as a leader and guide for all the ship's passengers, although he was one of the prisoners. This is the fourth time that Paul concerned himself with leading those with him in order to save them from death (vv. 10, 21, 31).
Paul encouraged those with him to eat, by giving thanks to God, praying before them, and beginning to eat.
The hearts of the ship's passengers were reassured and they rejoiced at Paul's confidence in his God, and they ate. The number of all of them was two hundred and seventy-six.

The presence of the children of God in a place is a source of comfort, joy, and deliverance for those present, as the history of the Church records that because of Anba Paula, the first hermit, God sent down dew and rain upon the land of Egypt.

So know that God desires to bless everyone around you for your sake if you live with Him faithfully, and God awaits your prayer for all, that He may have mercy on them, because you are His child and your place is great in His heart.

For the first time in two weeks, the ship's passengers ate their fill. And since they knew that the ship was about to sink, they made a final attempt to save themselves by lightening the load, so they threw the wheat into the sea, hoping that this would help the ship come closer to the shore and shorten the distance that they would have to drag it to the shore.

When the light of day appeared through the thick clouds, they saw a bay in a land they did not know, so they agreed to steer the ship toward it, and the sailors did not know that this was the island of Malta, because they were far from its harbor (ch. 28:1).
They cut the ropes that tie the anchors to the ship, and likewise loosed the ropes that tie the rudder, and hoisted a sail to take advantage of the wind's thrust of the ship toward the shore.
Two seas: two opposing currents of water.

The ship entered a place between two water currents, whose collision causes sand to be deposited as a tongue of sand in the sea, in which ships run aground and cannot be moved. This is what happened to the ship when they brought it close to the shore. As the bow stuck fast in the sand and the waves began to strike violently against the stern of the ship, its planks began to come apart from one another, that is, the ship broke up.
Roman law punished a soldier with death if his prisoner escaped, so the soldiers thought of killing the prisoners.

The centurion did not agree with the soldiers' opinion, in order to save Paul, whom he loved and treated kindly, and whose wisdom he was convinced of, and God's work in him through his guidance of the ship's passengers. So he commanded those of them who were able to swim to go down into the water and head for the shore.
The rest, that is, those who could not swim, clung to boards and pieces of wood from the ship, and floated on them until they reached the shore, and so all were saved.
This was the fourth time that Paul escaped drowning, for he had been shipwrecked three times before (2 Cor 11:25).

The servant who has a clear purpose continues in his ministry however often obstacles recur, and so it was with Paul, because his calling and his election were firm. So do not be troubled by the obstacles that face you, for this does not mean that God has forsaken you, but continue in your spiritual striving and your service, trusting in the power of your God to rescue you, knowing that your sins do not hinder God's work with you as long as you repent of them.
R.N From Malta to Rome
The ship's passengers were at last saved from drowning in the sea and reached the island of Malta, which lies south of Italy, and they learned its name from its inhabitants.

The people of the island of Malta were not Romans, and the Romans call them barbarians. They were distinguished by generosity, and they kindled a fire to warm them, especially after their exposure to the severe cold that prevailed on the island at that time and the rain that accompanied it.
Thus God arranges care for His children wherever they are, according to the generosity of His giving, so that they may be free of care.
Paul was gathering dry sticks to make the fire burn more, and a viper came out from among them, having been hiding from the cold, and fastened on his hand.

Those who watched the Apostle Paul thought that every sin has a punishment, so they imagined that divine justice was pursuing him for a crime of murder he had committed, so that when he escaped drowning, it followed him with the serpent's bite.
Paul cast the serpent into the fire and suffered no harm from its bite.

The barbarians watched Paul, waiting for him to die by swelling from the effect of the poison or to fall down suddenly, and they waited a long time to no avail, so their thoughts about him changed and they supposed him to be a god, that is, immortal, unaffected by poisons and not dying.

People's opinion is constantly changing from the far right to the far left, and if a person tries to please them completely, he will lose his discipleship of Christ (Gal 1:10). So do not be concerned with pleasing people at the expense of the truth, and do not be disturbed by their accusations against you if you are not in error and are submissive to the Church, but be concerned to please them for God's sake, so that you may win their souls for Him.

The foremost man of the island and its governor, whose name was Publius, owned lands around the place to which they had escaped. The man received them as guests and treated them kindly for three days.
Publius' father was sick with a high fever and severe diarrhea (a bloody flux = dysentery), so Paul went in and prayed and laid his hands on him, and Christ healed him.

The news of Paul's healing of Publius' father spread on the island, so people brought their sick to him, and he prayed over them and healed them, which made everyone honor Paul and those with him greatly. And when the time came for them to set sail, three months later, they gave them what they needed of provisions and clothing.

God gives with the temptation the way of escape. After days of drifting at sea and the feeling of being lost, relief came from the face of the Lord and they were treated with great honor, and Paul the prisoner came into great glory and became a cause of kindness to those who held him captive. So if the affliction increases, continue your prayers to God, who is able not only to rescue you but to change the affliction into great blessings. And if the offenses directed at you increase and you are even exposed to death like Paul, God is able to deliver you and to make you a cause of blessing for all who offended you, like the soldiers who wanted to kill Paul. But what matters is that you keep your love for those who harm you and your faith in your mighty God.
Castor and Pollux: the names of two gods whom sailors believe guard their ships at sea.
