After three months, they set sail from Malta and boarded a ship from Alexandria bearing the sign of Castor and Pollux. The ship had been anchored at the island during the winter, in which it is preferable not to travel.
The ship arrived at Syracuse, which is the capital of the island of Sicily and lies about eighty miles from Malta, and they stayed there three days.

The ship's sailors were compelled to go around in order to take advantage of the thrust of the wind, since it was contrary to their direction, so they arrived at Rhegium, a port in southern Italy. And after a day a south wind blew and drove them to Puteoli in western Italy.

In the city of Puteoli there were some Christians, so they received the ship's passengers as guests for a week, and perhaps it was an opportunity for Paul to reassure them, preach to them, and strengthen their faith. Then they moved on to Rome, which is about 140 miles from there.
Appii Forum: a market on the road between Puteoli and Rome, a hundred miles from Puteoli and forty miles from Rome. It is a place where people buy their needs, and so journeys stop there.
The Three Taverns: that is, three inns on the road to Rome after Appii Forum, about ten miles from Rome, and this place is considered a resting place for travelers.

A group of the Christians of Rome came out to meet them as far as the region of Appii Forum and the Three Taverns. Paul rejoiced at this reception and took courage, in return for what he had faced of imprisonment, trials, and shipwreck.

Dwelt by himself: Roman law allowed some prisoners of good repute to live in private houses of their own which they rented and not leave them, and they would be under guard, bound with chains to the soldiers guarding them.

When the journey reached Rome, Julius, the centurion, delivered the prisoners to the captain of the camp, and testified to Paul's greatness, his wisdom, and the power of his God, and also gave him Festus' letter, which testifies to the soundness of Paul's position, so the captain of the camp permitted him to dwell in a private house with the soldiers responsible for guarding him. Six soldiers were changed daily to guard Paul, each one's guard lasting four hours, during which he would be bound by a chain to Paul's hand.

God is able to give you favor in the eyes of those around you so that you may complete your spiritual striving and your service. So thank Him at all times, and make use of the blessings He bestows on you in order to draw near to Him.
After three days: from his arrival in Rome.

Paul hastened to begin preaching in Rome, so he sent and summoned the chief of the Jews to meet with them. At that time there were in Rome about sixty thousand Jews, who had seven synagogues and a quarter of their own. He told them that he was their brother and had done nothing against the Jews in Jerusalem or against the worship and the customs of the fathers, but that the Jews of Jerusalem had seized him and delivered him to the Romans, so he had come to Rome in bonds.
Paul told the chief of the Jews that the Romans had examined him and found him innocent, not deserving death on any account, and wished to release him.

The Jews opposed Paul and tried to kill him, so he was compelled to appeal his case to Caesar's court, because he was a Roman and had this right. In this he did not wish to bring his people to trial, but to stop the evil of these obstinate ones.

For this reason, Paul hastened to meet with the Jews of Rome, to see them and to confirm to them his message, from which it would become clear to them that the reason for his imprisonment is his faith in the Messiah, who is the hope of every Jew.

Since the time of Paul's voyage was in winter, when all the ships that carry news to other lands stop, they told him that nothing had yet reached them about him or his case from the Jews of Jerusalem.
This sect: Christianity.
The Jews asked him to set before them what he preaches, since they know that Christianity faces opposition everywhere.

A day was appointed for the meeting and a large number of Jews came to Paul's house, and he preached to them the Kingdom, of which the Law and the prophets prophesied, with prophecies and types concerning the Lord Jesus. This exposition continued for a whole day from beginning to end.
In the end, some of them were convinced of what was said and others were not convinced.

The Jews departed: divided among themselves, especially since Paul had ended his speech with what is in Isaiah (6:9-10) of God's words to him, declaring that the Jews would not hear the voice of God and would not discern it because of their obstinacy and the extreme hardness of their hearts, as if they feared hearing and understanding and returning to God to enjoy His blessings.
The salvation of God: the preaching of Christ the Savior.
Paul made clear to the Jews that God had sent the good news to the Gentiles, and that they would receive this preaching which the Jews themselves reject.
The Jews departed from Paul, and continued among themselves discussing what they had heard from Paul.

Paul continued preaching for two whole years (AD 61, 62) in Rome, settled in a house he had rented, and during them he preached to many Jews and Gentiles, among them Onesimus, the slave of Philemon (Phlm 10), who had come as a fugitive from his master who lived in Colossae. In it he sent the four prison epistles, to Philippi, Colossae, Ephesus, and Philemon. With him during them were Timothy, Luke the Evangelist, Epaphroditus, Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Tychicus, Justus, and Demas, as appears from the beginning and the end of the prison epistles.

Paul continued preaching Christ and the Kingdom without hindrance from the Romans, because they considered Christianity a sect of Judaism. Then they began their persecution of Christianity two years later, that is, in AD 64, after the Emperor Nero burned Rome and accused the Christians of it.

Paul preached while awaiting his trial without despair, anxiety, or complaint. God had permitted afflictions and prison for Paul, but He was with him, so he preached during them until he reached Rome and preached there. Thus the Book of Acts ends with the preaching reaching Rome, the capital of the empire, that is, the end of the earth, as Christ promised His disciples (ch. 1:8). After Paul's release from his first imprisonment in Rome, which is mentioned in this chapter, he preached in many places for five years. After that he was arrested and imprisoned in Rome for his second imprisonment, from which he sent his second epistle to Timothy, and then he was martyred in AD 68.

Do not waste your time on many things, so that you drift away from your goal, which is Christ. And let it not hinder you that some are not convinced by your words, but persevere in offering your love and your proclamation of Christ through all your life and your words, and God will support you and draw to Himself everyone who is ready to believe and to remain firm in the spiritual life because of you.
